Are FFS Medicare payments adequate 
in 2026?
Based on the most recently available data, indicators 
of the adequacy of IPPS and OPPS payments have been 
mixed. FFS Medicare beneficiaries maintained good 
access to hospital inpatient and outpatient services: 
Hospitals continued to have available capacity in 
aggregate, the supply of hospitals was relatively steady 
in both fiscal year (FY) 2024 and FY 2025, and FFS 
Medicare beneficiaries’ inpatient stays and hospital 
outpatient encounters per beneficiary increased. 
In addition, hospitals’ access to capital improved: 
Hospitals’ all-payer operating margin increased to 
6.5 percent in 2024, and preliminary data suggest a 
continued increase in 2025. However, the quality of 
hospital care was mixed: FFS Medicare beneficiaries’ 
risk-adjusted mortality rate improved in 2024, but 
their readmission rate worsened, and most patient-
experience measures remained stable. Hospitals’ FFS 
Medicare margin remained negative but increased 
to –12.1 percent in aggregate and to –1 percent for 
the median relatively efficient hospital. For 2026, we 
project hospitals’ FFS Medicare margin to increase to 
about –10 percent in aggregate and to 1 percent for the 
median relatively efficient hospital.
Beneficiaries maintained good access to 
hospital inpatient and outpatient services 
in 2024
Indicators of hospital capacity and supply and FFS 
Medicare beneficiaries’ use of services suggest that 
FFS Medicare beneficiaries maintained good access 
to hospital inpatient and outpatient services. In FY 
2024, hospitals continued to have available capacity in 
aggregate. The supply of hospitals was also relatively 
steady in both FY 2024 and FY 2025. Looking more 
specifically at FFS Medicare beneficiaries, the number 
of inpatient stays per beneficiary and hospital 
outpatient encounters per beneficiary both increased. 
Hospitals continued to have available capacity 
In FY 2024 hospitals continued to have available 
inpatient capacity in aggregate (Table 3-2). The number 
of inpatient beds remained relatively stable at about 
674,000 in FY 2024. Similarly, hospitals’ occupancy 
rate remained relatively stable at about 71 percent, 
indicating available inpatient capacity in aggregate. 
However, as in past years, there was significant 
variation within these aggregates, with some hospitals 
having substantially higher available capacity while 
others faced capacity constraints. For example, in FY 
2024, 5 percent of hospitals had an occupancy rate 
under 13 percent while another 5 percent had an 
occupancy rate over 90 percent; this variation was 
similar to FY 2023 (data not shown).
Hospital outpatient capacity is harder to measure, 
but two measures of timely and effective care suggest 
hospitals continued to have available emergency 
department (ED) capacity (Table 3-2). The median time 
from patients’ ED arrival to departure remained stable at 
about 150 minutes in FY 2024. While the median time is 
15 minutes higher than in 2019, it still suggests available 
ED capacity, especially as the median share of patients 
who left the ED without being seen has remained steady 
at 1 percent to 2 percent from calendar year (CY) 2019 
through CY 2023 (the most recent year of data currently 
available for that measure).
Overall hospital employment also continued to 
increase, reaching 4.8 million full-time-equivalent staff 
in FY 2024 (Table 3-2).
Supply of hospitals held relatively stable, though 
slightly more hospitals closed than opened
Since 2021 the supply of hospitals has been relatively 
stable, with about 4,530 unique provider numbers in FY 
2024 (Table 3-3, p. 70). Most hospitals continued to be 
short-term acute care hospitals, virtually all of which 
were paid by FFS Medicare under the IPPS and OPPS.5 
However, FFS Medicare beneficiaries also received care 
at 1,370 critical access hospitals, which are hospitals

with 25 or fewer beds that are generally located in rural 
areas and paid based on their costs. Additionally, since 
2023, FFS Medicare beneficiaries also receive care at a 
new type of hospital called a “rural emergency hospital” 
(REH). REHs are required to provide 24/7 ED services 
but are prohibited from furnishing acute inpatient care 
(see section at the end of this chapter on REHs, pp. 87–
88). The majority of hospitals continued to be located 
in urban areas and be nonprofit, and the number of 
nonprofit hospitals has continued to increase.
However, changes in the count of hospital provider 
numbers that provided FFS Medicare inpatient 
and outpatient services is an imperfect measure of 
changes in beneficiary access. For example, decreases 
in provider numbers can also reflect mergers and 
acquisitions without any change in the locations where 
beneficiaries can receive hospital services. On the 
other hand, hospitals opening new campuses can result 
in an increase in access without any change in the 
count of hospital provider numbers.
We therefore also look at changes in unique hospital 
locations where beneficiaries can receive hospital 
inpatient and emergency and other outpatient care; by 
this metric, eight more hospitals closed than opened in 
both FY 2024 and FY 2025 (Table 3-4, p. 71). In FY 2024,

additional 10 hospitals opened and 18 closed. Of the 10

32 miles (some data not shown). Of the 18 hospitals

number of rural hospital closures since 2023. Among 
the three rural nonmicropolitan hospitals that closed 
in FY 2025 (all of which were at least 25 miles from the 
next hospital), one is working to reopen as an REH, 
and the other two were not eligible to become an 
REH because they were not open in December 2020 (a 
condition for REH eligibility).

files.title: Service Line Operating Model
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 1.3
Service Line Operating Model
Tallowbrook Health | Office of the COO | 2025-11-12 | v1.3
This document describes how Tallowbrook organizes clinical services into service lines that 
cross our two hospitals and four outpatient facilities, and how responsibility is divided 
between service line leaders and facility leaders. It replaces version 1.2 (March 2024). The 
model itself has not changed since July 2023; this revision clarifies decision rights for 
capital requests and aligns the reporting cadence with the monthly operating review.
Why a matrix
Most of our clinical programs are delivered in more than one building. An orthopedic 
patient may be seen at an outpatient site, operated on at one of three surgical sites and 
rehabilitated at the Pavilion or Stafford.
Managing each building separately left no single owner for the patient's path, the physician 
relationships or the program's growth.
The service line model gives each program an owner across sites while facility presidents 
stay accountable for the people, space and budgets inside their buildings.
We accept the overhead of a matrix because reorganizing staff around programs would split 
small Hospital Fort Bend departments into units too small to staff reliably.
The seven service lines and where they operate
We recognize seven service lines. Their footprints differ, and several services are 
deliberately offered at one site only.
 Emergency & Hospital Medicine: 24-hour emergency departments at both hospitals (38 
treatment spaces at Medical Center West, 24 at Hospital Fort Bend) and hospitalist 
services.
 Surgical Services & Orthopedics: 10 operating rooms at Medical Center West, 6 at 
Hospital Fort Bend and the Surgery Center Grand Parkway.
 Heart & Vascular: cardiac catheterization at Medical Center West only; Hospital Fort 
Bend provides diagnostic cardiology and transfers STEMI patients to West by protocol.
 Women's & Infant Services: labor and delivery, Mother-Baby and the Level II NICU at 
Medical Center West only.
 Imaging & Diagnostics: hospital imaging at both campuses, outpatient imaging at the 
Pavilion and Stafford, and lab draw sites. Outpatient mammography sits here.
 Rehabilitation & Therapy: inpatient therapy at both hospitals and outpatient therapy at 
the Pavilion and Stafford.
 Primary & Urgent Care: Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.3
Dyad leadership and councils
Each service line is led by a physician leader and an administrative director working as a 
dyad.
The physician leader owns clinical standards, physician engagement and program 
development. The administrator owns operating plans, volumes and coordination with 
facility leaders.
Each line has a council that meets quarterly: the dyad, nursing directors of the units most 
involved, representatives from both hospitals and Decision Support.
Councils review volumes, access, quality measures and the quarterly contribution report, 
and they propose program changes. They do not approve budgets.
Decision rights: service line versus facility
The division of decision rights below is the part of the model most often misunderstood.
 Facility presidents decide staffing levels, hiring, unit assignments, space use and the 
facility operating budget.
 Service line dyads recommend program additions, equipment standards and physician 
recruitment priorities; the COO approves after the affected facility president reviews 
operating impact.
 Capital requests for program equipment are sponsored jointly: the service line sets 
clinical priority and the facility confirms space, utilities and staffing.
 Cross-site clinical protocols, such as STEMI transfers from Hospital Fort Bend, are 
owned by the service line and adopted by each medical staff.
Attribution and reporting rules
Encounters are attributed to one service line by primary service or principal procedure. An 
orthopedic surgery admission counts in Surgical Services & Orthopedics even if the patient 
spends a night in the ICU.
Emergency visits count in Emergency & Hospital Medicine unless the patient is admitted; 
the inpatient stay is then attributed by service.
Decision Support produces contribution margin by service line quarterly from the 
enterprise data warehouse, using the finance cost-allocation rules for overhead.
Contribution reports inform program decisions. They are not used in individual 
compensation.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.3
Review cadence
Service line results appear in the monthly operating review on the third Thursday alongside 
facility results.
Councils meet quarterly, and each dyad presents an annual plan during the February-to-
May budget cycle.
The board's Finance & Operations Committee sees service line results in its monthly review 
and receives a fuller service line report twice a year.
What the model does not cover
Tallowbrook has no inpatient behavioral health beds. Emergency psychiatric consultation 
comes from a tele-psychiatry partner, and patients needing admission are transferred to 
area behavioral health hospitals.
Behavioral health is managed within Emergency & Hospital Medicine rather than as a 
separate line.
Neither hospital is a Level I or II trauma center; major trauma is transferred to regional 
centers.
The Surgery Center Grand Parkway takes part in the surgical council but is governed by its 
own joint venture board.

files.title: Tallowbrook Health: Organization Overview
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 2026.2
Tallowbrook Health: Organization 
Overview
Tallowbrook Health | Strategy & Communications | 2026-08-15 | v2026.2
Tallowbrook Health is a community-governed, nonprofit health system serving west 
Houston and Fort Bend County. This overview is written for advisers, prospective partners 
and others who need a factual picture of who we are, where we operate and what we do. It 
reflects the organization as of August 2026.
Who we are
Tallowbrook Community Health System, known as Tallowbrook Health, is a Texas nonprofit 
corporation exempt under section 501(c)(3). Our offices are in west Houston.
We began as a single community hospital. Medical Center West opened in 1979, and we 
opened Hospital Fort Bend in Richmond in 2017 as families moved south and west.
Our outpatient sites followed the same pattern: the Surgery Center Grand Parkway in 2018, 
Mission Bend in 2019 and Imaging & Therapy Stafford in 2021.
We are one of 2,984 nongovernment not-for-profit community hospitals counted in the 
American Hospital Association's most recent national survey, which found 5,121 
community hospitals in all.
Where we operate
We operate six facilities in Harris and Fort Bend counties.
 Tallowbrook Medical Center West (Harris County): 214 licensed beds, 24-hour 
emergency department, labor and delivery with a Level II NICU, cardiac catheterization 
and 10 operating rooms.
 Tallowbrook Hospital Fort Bend (Richmond): 112 licensed beds, 24-hour emergency 
department and 6 operating rooms.
 Tallowbrook Outpatient Pavilion West, next to Medical Center West: imaging, an 18-
chair infusion center, outpatient therapy and lab draw.
 Tallowbrook Surgery Center Grand Parkway (Fort Bend County): an ambulatory 
surgery center with four operating rooms and two procedure rooms, owned jointly with 
physician partners.
 Tallowbrook Imaging & Therapy Stafford: MRI, CT, ultrasound, mammography, DEXA 
and physical therapy.
Tallowbrook Health • 2026.2
 Tallowbrook Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend: urgent care from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. 
every day, primary care, X-ray and lab draw.
What we offer
Our clinical services are organized into seven service lines that work across our facilities, so 
patients can move between sites without starting over:
 Emergency & Hospital Medicine
 Surgical Services & Orthopedics
 Heart & Vascular
 Women's & Infant Services
 Imaging & Diagnostics
 Rehabilitation & Therapy
 Primary & Urgent Care
Scale and people
At the end of our 2026 fiscal year (July 1, 2025 to June 30, 2026) we employed about 3,080 
people, or 2,650 full-time equivalents, including about 1,015 registered nurse FTEs.
About 790 physicians and advanced practice providers hold privileges at our hospitals. 
Most are in independent practice in the communities we serve.
Governance and mission
A 13-member community board governs Tallowbrook. Its Finance & Operations Committee 
meets monthly, and the full board approves our budget each June.
As a nonprofit, we reinvest in the communities we serve. Current programs include 
emergency department navigation to primary care for patients without a regular doctor, 
transportation vouchers and diabetes education classes at Mission Bend.
What we do not provide
We want partners to understand our limits as well as our services.
Neither of our hospitals is a Level I or Level II trauma center. Patients with major trauma 
are taken to, or transferred to, regional trauma centers.
We do not operate inpatient behavioral health beds. Emergency psychiatric consultation is 
available through a tele-psychiatry partner, and patients who need admission are 
transferred to area behavioral health hospitals.

Service Lines at Tallowbrook Health
Tallowbrook Health | Strategy & Communications | 2026-07-01
This guide helps referring physicians, community partners and patients find the right Tallowbrook
service and location. Each entry explains what is offered, where, and how to arrange care. Services
are organized into seven service lines that work across our two hospitals and four outpatient
facilities in west Houston and Fort Bend County.
Finding the right care
For emergencies, go to the nearest emergency department or call 911. Both Tallowbrook hospitals
have 24-hour emergency departments.
For scheduled imaging, infusion and therapy, one central scheduling team books appointments at
the Outpatient Pavilion West, Imaging & Therapy Stafford and hospital outpatient imaging. Surgery
Center Grand Parkway cases are scheduled through the surgeon's office with the center directly.
Emergency and hospital medicine
Medical Center West has a 38-space emergency department with Level IV trauma designation;
Hospital Fort Bend has a 24-space emergency department. Hospitalists care for admitted adult
patients at both hospitals.
Patients with major trauma are taken to or transferred to regional Level I and II trauma centers.
Emergency psychiatric consultation is available through our tele-psychiatry partner; patients who
need inpatient behavioral health care are transferred to area specialty hospitals.
Surgery and orthopedics
Surgery is available at three sites: Medical Center West (10 operating rooms), Hospital Fort Bend (6
operating rooms) and the Surgery Center Grand Parkway (4 operating rooms and 2 procedure
rooms). Services include orthopedics and spine, general surgery, gynecologic surgery, urology and
ear, nose and throat surgery.
Heart and vascular
Cardiac catheterization is performed in two labs at Medical Center West. Hospital Fort Bend offers
diagnostic cardiology and transfers patients with a STEMI heart attack to Medical Center West
under an established protocol.
Women's and infant services
Labor and delivery, Mother-Baby care and a 10-bassinet Level II NICU are located at Medical
Center West. Hospital Fort Bend does not provide obstetric care and refers expectant mothers to
Medical Center West. Screening mammography is offered at the Pavilion and Stafford through
Imaging & Diagnostics.

Imaging and diagnostics
Outpatient imaging is available at the Outpatient Pavilion West (MRI, CT, ultrasound,
mammography and X-ray) and Imaging & Therapy Stafford (MRI, CT, ultrasound, mammography
and DEXA). Both hospitals provide imaging for emergency and inpatient care. Lab draw stations
are located at the Pavilion and Mission Bend.
Rehabilitation and therapy
Physical and occupational therapists see inpatients at both hospitals. Outpatient physical and
occupational therapy is offered at the Pavilion, and outpatient physical therapy at Stafford.
Primary and urgent care
Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend offers walk-in urgent care from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. every day,
primary care appointments with six providers, X-ray and lab draw.
Scheduling and referrals
Referring offices can send imaging, infusion and therapy orders to central scheduling, which
contacts the patient to book. Patients receive automated reminders 72 and 24 hours before their
visit, and schedulers call imaging patients who need preparation instructions.
Emergency care: no appointment needed at either hospital.
Surgery: scheduled by the surgeon's office with the chosen surgical site.
Imaging, infusion and outpatient therapy: central scheduling.
Primary care at Mission Bend: call the clinic or walk in for urgent care.

files.title: Surgical & Orthopedic Care at Tallowbrook

Surgical & Orthopedic Care at Tallowbrook
Tallowbrook Health | Strategy & Communications | 2026-08-01
Whether you need a joint replaced, a hernia repaired or a same-day procedure, Tallowbrook offers
surgery close to home in west Houston and Fort Bend County. This sheet explains where surgery is
done, what we offer and how to prepare.
Care close to home
Surgical Services & Orthopedics is one of Tallowbrook's seven service lines. Surgeons, nurses and
therapists work across our sites so your care follows you from the first visit through recovery.
Three places for surgery
Your surgeon will recommend the site that fits your procedure and health needs.
Tallowbrook Medical Center West: 10 operating rooms for inpatient and outpatient surgery, with
intensive care and cardiac services on site.
Tallowbrook Hospital Fort Bend in Richmond: 6 operating rooms for inpatient and outpatient
surgery.
Tallowbrook Surgery Center Grand Parkway: 4 operating rooms and 2 procedure rooms for
same-day surgery, operated with physician partners.
Common procedures
Our surgeons perform joint replacement, sports medicine and arthroscopy, spine surgery, general
and laparoscopic surgery, gynecologic surgery, urology and ear, nose and throat procedures. Ask
your surgeon which site offers your procedure.
Before your procedure
Your surgeon's office schedules the procedure. A nurse will call you a few days ahead to review
your medicines, arrival time and instructions about eating and drinking. Bring a photo ID, your
insurance card and a list of your medicines, and arrange for an adult to drive you home after
same-day surgery.
After surgery
Many patients go home the same day. If you stay overnight, you will recover on a surgical unit at
Medical Center West or Hospital Fort Bend. Outpatient physical therapy is available at the
Outpatient Pavilion West and at Imaging & Therapy Stafford.

When we refer elsewhere
Tallowbrook hospitals are not Level I or Level II trauma centers. Patients with major injuries are
taken to regional trauma centers, and some highly specialized procedures are referred to academic
medical centers in Houston.

FY2026 Year-End Operating Summary
Tallowbrook Health | Office of the COO | 2026-09-10 | v1.0 (board package, 
September 2026)
This summary reports Tallowbrook's operating results for the fiscal year ended June 30, 
2026, with July and August 2026 trends, for the Finance & Operations Committee meeting 
on September 17. Financial results are unaudited; the audit is expected in October. Volume 
figures come from the facility activity series maintained by Decision Support.
Headlines
 Inpatient admissions rose 1.0% to 16,651; growth came entirely from Hospital Fort 
Bend (+7.2%), while Medical Center West was 2.2% lower.
 Emergency visits rose 3.2% to 105,599, and outpatient imaging and visits grew fastest 
at Stafford (about +8%).
 Operating income was $8.6 million on $618.4 million of net operating revenue, a 1.4% 
margin against a 2.1% budget.
 Agency nursing hours fell at both hospitals after the Central Staffing Office started, and 
the RN vacancy rate fell to 11.8%.
 July and August 2026 volumes are running above the same months last year at both 
hospitals.

emergency visits (+1.5%), 8,370 surgical cases and 2,399 births.

(+5.6%) and 4,589 surgical cases.
The Surgery Center Grand Parkway performed 6,252 cases (+0.8%). The Pavilion 
performed 30,740 imaging exams (+2.5%) and 73,863 other outpatient visits (+3.6%).
Imaging & Therapy Stafford performed 44,825 imaging exams (+8.3%) and 19,218 therapy 
and other visits (+8.2%). Mission Bend recorded 41,653 clinic and urgent care visits 
(+3.7%).

FTEs. The hospital RN vacancy rate was 11.8% at June 30, down from 14.9% a year earlier.

Net operating revenue was $618.4 million, up 5.2% from $587.9 million in FY2025. 
Operating expenses were $609.8 million, leaving operating income of $8.6 million (1.4%) 
against a budgeted 2.1%. FY2025 operating income was $12.3 million (2.1%).
Salaries, wages and benefits were about 48% of expense, supplies 16%, purchased services 
and other 30%, and depreciation and interest 6%.

files.title: Patient Placement and Bed Management Procedure — Medical Center West
files.filename: Patient Placement and Bed Management Procedure — Medical Center West.docx
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 4.2
Patient Placement and Bed 
Management Procedure — Medical 
Center West
Tallowbrook Health | Capacity Management, Medical Center West | 2025-
09-15 | v4.2
Procedure CM-104, revision 4.2. Applies to all inpatient placements at Tallowbrook Medical 
Center West, including admissions from the emergency department, direct admissions, 
post-procedure admissions and internal transfers. Revision 4.2 updates the escalation 
contacts and restates the boarding measurement definition; the workflow is unchanged 
from revision 4.1.
Scope
This procedure covers the 192 staffed inpatient beds at Medical Center West: ICU (20), 
Progressive Care (24), Telemetry (28), 4 West (32), 5 West (30), 6 West 
Surgical/Orthopedic (28), Mother-Baby (20) and NICU (10).
Labor and delivery triage, the NICU admission process and transfers to outside facilities 
follow their own procedures. They are referenced here only where they affect bed 
assignment.
Roles
 House supervisor: assigns beds 24 hours a day using the EHR bed board and approves 
placements outside a patient's preferred unit.
 Capacity management manager: leads the daily bed huddle, owns escalation during 
business hours and reviews exceptions weekly.
 Unit charge nurse: updates bed status, confirms expected discharges and accepts 
assigned patients.
 Case management: identifies expected discharges and barriers by 9:00 a.m.
 Environmental services lead: cleans vacated beds in priority order set by the house 
supervisor.
 Transport: moves patients after a bed is assigned and ready.
Bed request to assignment
 1. The admitting provider enters the admission order in the EHR; the order creates the 
bed request.
Tallowbrook Health • 4.2
 2. The house supervisor reviews level of care and isolation needs and assigns a bed on 
the EHR bed board.
 3. The receiving charge nurse accepts or raises a concern within 15 minutes.
 4. When the bed is marked clean and ready, the ED nurse gives report and transport is 
requested.
 5. The patient's arrival on the unit is recorded in the EHR, which closes the request.
Daily bed huddle
The bed huddle is held at 9:30 a.m. every day in the capacity office, with a phone bridge for 
unit charge nurses.
Attendees are the capacity management manager (lead), unit charge nurses, case 
management, the environmental services lead and transport.
Each unit reports open beds, expected discharges, pending admissions and staffing 
concerns. The huddle agrees on the order of discharges and bed cleaning.
When house occupancy is above 85%, a second check-in is held at 2:30 p.m.
Escalation
A bed request that is not assigned within 60 minutes is escalated by the house supervisor to 
the capacity management manager, or after hours to the administrator on call.
 Step 1: review expected discharges and request early discharge support from case 
management.
 Step 2: consider placement on an alternate unit with appropriate nursing competency.
 Step 3: open overflow capacity approved by the chief nursing officer.
 Step 4: the administrator on call decides on diversion status with the ED medical 
director.
Boarding measurement
ED boarding time runs from the inpatient admission order to the time the patient physically 
leaves the ED for an inpatient bed.
Boarding hours are attributed to the destination unit, not the ED, and are reported daily by 
Decision Support.
Reports before February 2024 started the clock at the bed request rather than the 
admission order, so older boarding figures are not directly comparable.
Exceptions and special populations
Patients requiring isolation are placed only in rooms marked for isolation on the bed board.
Tallowbrook Health • 4.2
Pediatric patients admitted through the ED are placed according to the pediatric admission 
criteria in the ED procedure manual.
Patients awaiting transfer to a behavioral health hospital remain under ED care unless a 
medical admission is ordered.
Records
Bed requests, assignments and transfer times are recorded in the EHR ADT and bed 
management module and loaded nightly to the data warehouse. Huddle notes are kept by 
the capacity office for 90 days.

files.title: Bed Huddle and Capacity Escalation Guideline — Hospital Fort Bend
files.filename: Bed Huddle and Capacity Escalation Guideline — Hospital Fort Bend.pdf
files.search:
Bed Huddle and Capacity Escalation Guideline —
 Hospital Fort Bend
Tallowbrook Health | Nursing, Hospital Fort Bend | 2024-11-01
Guideline NS-FB-22, version 2.0, effective November 1, 2024. This guideline sets out the daily bed
huddle and the three capacity levels used at Tallowbrook Hospital Fort Bend. It replaces the March
2021 version, which relied on ad hoc calls to the house supervisor.
Purpose
Hospital Fort Bend has 96 staffed beds on four units: ICU (12), 2 North Medical-Surgical (32), 3
North Medical-Surgical/Telemetry (30) and 3 South Surgical (22). Because the hospital is small, a
few unexpected admissions can fill a unit quickly. The capacity levels give everyone the same
signal and the same next steps.
Daily 10:00 huddle
The house supervisor leads a 15-minute huddle at 10:00 a.m. every day with unit charge nurses,
case management, environmental services and the ED charge nurse. Each unit reports open beds,
expected discharges and pending admissions from the EHR bed board. The house supervisor
declares the capacity level for the day and re-declares it whenever conditions change.
Green level
Green applies when occupancy is below 80% and no admitted patient has waited in the ED more
than two hours for a bed.
Routine placement by the house supervisor.
Case management confirms expected discharges by noon.
Elective surgical admissions proceed as scheduled.
Yellow level
Yellow applies when occupancy is 80% to 90%, or two or more admitted patients have waited in the
ED more than two hours.
House supervisor notifies the chief nursing officer and the ED medical director.
Case management and hospitalists review all expected discharges before 11:00 a.m.
Environmental services prioritizes discharge cleans over routine work.
House supervisor arranges additional nursing staff through the unit call-off list or overtime.

Red level
Red applies when occupancy is above 90%, the ICU has no open bed, or four or more admitted
patients have waited in the ED more than four hours.
Chief nursing officer or administrator on call joins a capacity call within 30 minutes.
Elective inpatient surgical cases for the next day are reviewed with Perioperative Services.
Transfers of suitable patients to Medical Center West are considered with the West capacity
manager.
Diversion is requested only by the administrator on call with the ED medical director.
Transfers to Medical Center West
Patients needing services not available at Hospital Fort Bend, including interventional cardiology for
STEMI and obstetric care, are transferred to Medical Center West under existing protocols
regardless of capacity level. Capacity-related transfers require acceptance by a West physician and
the West house supervisor.
Review
The nursing leadership team reviews the thresholds annually or after any red-level day that lasts
more than 12 hours. Questions go to the Hospital Fort Bend chief nursing officer.

files.title: West Capacity & Patient Flow Program: Charter and Design
files.filename: West Capacity & Patient Flow Program: Charter and Design.docx
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 1.0
West Capacity & Patient Flow Program: 
Charter and Design
Tallowbrook Health | Performance Improvement Office | 2026-01-28 | v1.0
Charter approved by the operating committee on January 28, 2026. Sponsor: Victor Salinas, 
President, Medical Center West. Program lead: Hannah Mercer, Performance Improvement. 
Operational lead: Aaron Foster, Capacity Management. This charter defines a six-month 
pilot on three medical units and the measures that will decide whether to spread it.
Background
Medical Center West ran at 72.5% average occupancy in FY2025, but monthly occupancy 
reached 80.2% in January 2025 and 82.7% in February 2025. On the busiest days, admitted 
patients waited in the ED for medical beds.
December 2025 occupancy was 75.9%. The current placement procedure and 9:30 a.m. 
huddle work, but most discharges happen in the afternoon, after the day's ED admissions 
start to queue.
Staff on 4 West, 5 West and Telemetry describe discharge planning that starts late in the 
stay and depends on individual physicians.
Aim
By August 31, 2026, 30% of discharges from the three pilot units will occur before 11:00 
a.m., without an increase in readmission concerns raised through case management.
Secondary aim: reduce ED boarding hours attributed to the pilot units compared with the 
same months of 2025, recognizing that boarding also depends on season and ED volume.
Scope
In scope: 4 West Medical-Surgical (32 beds), 5 West Medical-Surgical (30 beds) and 
Telemetry (28 beds) at Medical Center West, from March 2, 2026.
Out of scope: the ICU, Progressive Care, 6 West, Mother-Baby, the NICU and all Hospital Fort 
Bend units. The placement procedure itself is not being rewritten during the pilot.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.0
Changes to test
 Expected discharge date entered in the EHR by the end of hospital day 2 and updated 
daily.
 A next-day discharge list agreed on each unit by 3:00 p.m., shared with transport and 
pharmacy.
 Standard work for the 9:30 a.m. bed huddle: each pilot unit reports discharges planned 
before 11:00 a.m. and barriers to them.
 Environmental services notified when a patient leaves, rather than when the room is 
released in the EHR.
Measures
Measures follow the operational metric definitions standard.
 Outcome: share of discharges completed before 11:00 a.m., weekly by unit.
 Outcome: ED boarding hours attributed to pilot units, by month.
 Process: share of patients with an expected discharge date by day 2.
 Balancing: readmission concerns and complaints logged by case management.
 Context: unit midnight occupancy, including observation patients.
Team and roles
 Sponsor: President, Medical Center West.
 Program lead: Director, Performance Improvement.
 Operational lead: Manager, Capacity Management.
 Unit leads: nurse managers of 4 West, 5 West and Telemetry.
 Members: hospitalist group lead, case management manager, environmental services 
manager, Decision Support analyst.
Timeline
 February 2026: baseline data pull and unit training.
 March 2, 2026: pilot go-live.
 Late March 2026: next-day discharge list available in the EHR.
 June 2026: 90-day review.
 September 2026: evaluation and recommendation to the operating committee.
Risks and assumptions
Baseline figures for discharge timing will be finalized after the February data pull; the pre-
pilot baseline covers only one month and will be noisy.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.0
Summer occupancy is normally lower than winter occupancy, so comparing pilot months 
with February will overstate any improvement in boarding. The evaluation must account 
for season.
The EHR discharge list depends on the IS build queue. A paper list will be used until it is 
available.

files.title: Surgical Block Scheduling Policy
files.search:
Surgical Block Scheduling Policy
Tallowbrook Health | Perioperative Services | 2025-08-01
Policy PS-210, revision 3, effective August 1, 2025. Approved by the perioperative committee and
the medical executive committees of Tallowbrook Medical Center West and Hospital Fort Bend.
Revision 3 lengthens the release window for orthopedics and spine and restates how utilization is
measured.
Purpose and scope
This policy governs access to operating room time at Medical Center West (10 operating rooms)
and Hospital Fort Bend (6 operating rooms). The Surgery Center Grand Parkway is governed by its
own board and scheduling rules and is not covered.
The aims are fair access for surgeons, predictable staffing for perioperative teams and full use of
staffed operating room time.
Definitions
Block: a recurring period of staffed operating room time assigned to a surgical service.
Released time: block time given back by the service before the release deadline.
Open time: unassigned staffed time plus released time, booked first come, first served.
Block utilization: in-room to out-of-room minutes used within the block, divided by allocated minutes
minus minutes released on time.
Allocation
Blocks are allocated to services, not to individual surgeons. Each service chief distributes the
service's blocks among surgeons and informs Perioperative Services by the 15th of the prior month.
New services or surgeons request time through the Director of Perioperative Services. Requests
are considered at the next quarterly review.
Release rules
Unused block time must be released at least 72 hours before the day of surgery. Orthopedics and
spine must release at least five business days ahead, because implant and equipment scheduling
needs more notice.
Time not released by the deadline and not used counts against the service's utilization.
Open and released time

Released and unassigned time is posted in the EHR surgery schedule and booked first come, first
served by any credentialed surgeon. Add-on and urgent cases are scheduled by the OR charge
nurse according to case urgency and are not charged to a block.
Quarterly review
The perioperative committee reviews utilization by service each quarter. A service below 70% block
utilization for two consecutive quarters is reviewed for reallocation. The committee may reduce the
allocation, convert it to open time or keep it with a documented reason, such as a new surgeon
building a practice.
Exceptions
The chief medical officer of either hospital may suspend block rules during an emergency or a mass
casualty event. Robotic room scheduling will be addressed in a future revision.

files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 1.0
Recommendation: FY2027 Block 
Adjustments
Tallowbrook Health | Perioperative Services | 2026-09-15 | v1.0
To: Gregory Tanaka, COO; Janelle Brooks, President, Hospital Fort Bend; Victor Salinas, 
President, Medical Center West. From: Colleen Park, Director, Perioperative Services, on 
behalf of the perioperative committee. Date: September 15, 2026.
Decision requested
Approve three block changes effective with the January 2027 schedule, so surgeons and 
staff have more than 90 days' notice.
Recommendation
 Move one weekly half-day (four-hour) block from Hospital Fort Bend General Surgery to 
Hospital Fort Bend Orthopedics.
 Return one weekly half-day Medical Center West ENT block to open time.
 Keep Hospital Fort Bend Gynecology's allocation for one more quarter, with weekly 
release reminders, and review again in January.
Evidence
Policy PS-210 calls for review when a service is below 70% utilization for two consecutive 
quarters. Three services met that test in FY2026.
Fort Bend General Surgery ran at 66.7% for the year and below 70% in every quarter. It 
released 16.3% of its time, the highest share of any service.
West ENT ran at 63.9% for the year, between 62.6% and 65.2% each quarter.
Fort Bend Gynecology ran at 69.5%, below 70% in the last three quarters, during which one 
surgeon was on extended leave.
Fort Bend Orthopedics ran at 90.2% and was above 88% every quarter, and has asked twice 
for more time.

files.filename: Central Scheduling Standard Work: Outpatient Imaging.docx
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 2.1
Central Scheduling Standard Work: 
Outpatient Imaging
Tallowbrook Health | Patient Access & Central Scheduling | 2025-06-02 | 
v2.1
Standard work PA-031, version 2.1, effective June 2, 2025. Applies to central schedulers 
booking outpatient imaging at the Outpatient Pavilion West, Imaging & Therapy Stafford 
and hospital outpatient imaging. Version 2.1 incorporates lessons from the imaging 
scheduling consolidation completed in April 2025.
Scope
Covers MRI, CT, ultrasound, mammography, DEXA and X-ray orders for outpatients. 
Emergency and inpatient imaging is scheduled by the hospital imaging departments.
Outpatient therapy scheduling remains with site front desks until it moves to central 
scheduling.
Order intake
 1. Orders arrive through the EHR referral queue, the scheduling fax line or the referral 
portal.
 2. The intake scheduler confirms the order is signed, the exam is specific and diagnosis 
information is present.
 3. Incomplete orders go back to the ordering office the same day with the missing item 
named.
 4. Orders needing prior authorization are routed to the authorization team before 
scheduling.
Scheduling the exam
 Offer the first available slot at the patient's preferred site, then the other site.
 Book in the EHR enterprise scheduling module; never hold a slot outside the system.
 Contrast exams need the eGFR rule check before booking.
 Book mammography and DEXA together when both are ordered.
Preparation calls
Schedulers call every patient whose exam needs preparation, such as fasting, contrast 
screening or implant checks for MRI, at least two business days before the exam.
Tallowbrook Health • 2.1
Use the modality prep script in the scheduler reference guide. Document the call outcome in 
the appointment notes.
Reminders and confirmations
Automated text or voice reminders go out 72 and 24 hours before the appointment. Patients 
who reply to cancel are offered a new time by the next scheduler on shift, and the slot is 
released.
Exceptions
 Walk-in patients with orders: site staff call the scheduling lead line; schedulers book the 
next available slot the same day if possible.
 Urgent orders from physicians: book within two business days or escalate to the 
imaging lead.
 Interpreter needs: book the interpreter at the time of scheduling.
Measures
Scheduling leads review slots offered, booked and completed and third-next-available 
appointment for each schedule every Monday, using the weekly access dashboard.

files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 1.0
Central Staffing Office Operating 
Procedure
Tallowbrook Health | Central Staffing Office | 2025-10-20 | v1.0
Procedure CSO-001, version 1.0, effective October 20, 2025, the go-live date of the Central 
Staffing Office at Tallowbrook Medical Center West. It describes how nurse staffing is 
balanced across units each day. Hospital Fort Bend and outpatient sites will be added in 
Phase 2; steps for them are marked as Phase 2.
Purpose and scope
The Central Staffing Office (CSO) matches nursing staff to patient needs across the eight 
Medical Center West inpatient units and the emergency department.
It manages the float pool, balances staffing twice a day, approves premium pay and handles 
agency requests.
Unit staffing targets come from the official nurse services staffing plan. The CSO does not 
change those targets; it fills them.
Roles
 CSO director: owns the procedure, the float pool budget and agency usage reporting.
 Staffing coordinators: run the daily huddles, deploy float staff and record changes in the 
workforce scheduling system.
 Unit charge nurses: report census, acuity and staffing gaps before each huddle.
 House supervisors: make staffing decisions between huddles and overnight.
 Nurse managers: publish unit schedules six weeks ahead and approve schedule changes.
Daily staffing huddles
Huddles are held at 5:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. by phone bridge. Each unit reports expected 
census and acuity for the next shift, scheduled staff and gaps compared with the staffing 
plan grid.
The coordinator proposes moves in this order: float pool staff, voluntary moves between 
units, extra shifts by part-time staff, overtime, then agency.
Requests and deployment
 1. Charge nurse enters the gap in the workforce scheduling system before the huddle.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.0
 2. Coordinator assigns a float nurse or approves a unit-to-unit move and updates the 
schedule.
 3. Float staff receive assignments by text and report to the unit charge nurse.
 4. Unfilled gaps are escalated to the house supervisor with the options already tried.
Premium pay approval
Overtime and incentive shifts need CSO approval before the shift starts, except in 
emergencies approved by the house supervisor.
Approvals are recorded with a pay code in the workforce scheduling system, which sends 
worked hours to payroll each pay period.
Agency requests
Agency nurses are used only after internal options are exhausted and require CSO approval. 
Tallowbrook uses two staffing agencies under one master agreement; requests go to the 
agency with the matching credential first.
Records and reporting
The CSO keeps a daily deployment log and reports float, overtime and agency hours by unit 
after each pay period.
The nurse staffing committee receives these figures for its semiannual evaluation of the 
staffing plan against actual staffing.
Phase 2
Hospital Fort Bend units will request float staff through the CSO in Phase 2. Until then, Fort 
Bend house supervisors continue to manage staffing gaps locally.

files.title: Nurse Staffing Plan Evaluation, January–June 2026
files.search:
Nurse Staffing Plan Evaluation, January–June 2026
Tallowbrook Health | Nursing Services | 2026-08-18
Semiannual report of the nurse staffing committees of Tallowbrook Medical Center West and
Tallowbrook Hospital Fort Bend to the Board of Directors, submitted by the System Chief Nursing
Officer. This report covers the 13 pay periods from January 4 through July 4, 2026 and compares
the official nurse services staffing plans with actual RN staffing.
Requirement and scope
Texas Health and Safety Code Chapter 257 requires each hospital to adopt an official nurse
services staffing plan based on the needs of each patient care unit and shift. It requires a nurse
staffing committee with at least 60% direct-care registered nurses that meets at least quarterly and
evaluates the plan at least semiannually.
This evaluation covers the 12 inpatient units and both emergency departments. Planned hours are
the staffing plan grids applied to each unit's actual census; worked hours include overtime, float
pool and agency hours.
Committee activity
Both committees met in February and May 2026. Each has a direct-care RN majority selected by
peers.
The committees reviewed staffing concerns raised through the concern form, the unit grids for
Telemetry and 3 North, and the effect of the Central Staffing Office, which opened at Medical
Center West in October 2025 and began serving Hospital Fort Bend units on February 16, 2026.
Planned versus actual staffing
Across both hospitals, 463,181 RN hours were worked against 455,155 planned, 1.8% above plan.
For July to December 2025 the variance was 1.2% above plan.
Medical Center West: 1.5% above plan.
Hospital Fort Bend: 2.2% above plan.
Largest unit variances: Hospital Fort Bend emergency department (2.6%), Hospital Fort Bend ICU
(2.4%) and 2 North (2.2%).
Smallest: Medical Center West Mother-Baby (0.9%) and 5 West (1.1%).
No unit worked fewer hours than planned over the period.
Premium labor and float pool

Overtime was 5.5% of worked hours, float pool 5.2% and agency 3.8%. In July to December 2025
the figures were 6.0%, 3.4% and 5.5%.
At Medical Center West, overtime was 4.9% and agency 2.8%. At Hospital Fort Bend, overtime was
6.6% and agency 5.7%; Fort Bend's agency share has fallen since it joined the Central Staffing
Office but remains about twice West's.
Workforce context
Tallowbrook's hospital RN position vacancy rate was 11.8% at June 30, 2026, down from 14.9% a
year earlier. For comparison, the 2024 Texas Hospital Nurse Staffing Study reported a statewide
RN vacancy rate of 16.4% and a median hospital RN turnover rate of 23.2%.
Like most Texas hospitals in that study, we use shift differentials and flexible scheduling for
retention.
Committee findings
The staffing plans are being met; staffing above plan is concentrated at Hospital Fort Bend and
reflects higher census in January and February.
The Telemetry grid remains appropriate after review; the 3 North grid will add a charge nurse
without an assignment on day shift when census exceeds 26.
Staff report that float nurses arrive with better orientation since the CSO started.
Nurse-sensitive quality indicators are reported separately in the quality report.
Recommendations to the board
Accept the staffing plans for both hospitals for July to December 2026 with the 3 North change.
Continue Central Staffing Office Phase 2, including float pool growth for Hospital Fort Bend.
Receive the next evaluation in February 2027.

files.title: Procurement and Value Analysis Policy
files.search:
Procurement and Value Analysis Policy
Tallowbrook Health | Supply Chain | 2024-03-01
Policy SC-100, Revision 5. Owner: Vice President, Supply Chain. Approved by the Chief Financial
Officer. Effective March 1, 2024; supersedes Revision 4 (July 2023). Applies to all Tallowbrook
Health departments and facilities.
1. Purpose
This policy sets out how Tallowbrook buys supplies, equipment and services: who may request and
approve a purchase, when a contract must be used, and how new products are evaluated before
they are added to inventory or purchased repeatedly.
2. Scope
The policy covers non-pharmacy purchases of supplies, minor equipment, purchased services and
maintenance agreements. Pharmaceuticals follow the Pharmacy purchasing procedure. Capital
projects follow the Capital Budget policy, and physician agreements, real estate leases and
software licenses are managed by their owning departments.
3. Requisition to receipt
All purchases start as a requisition in the ERP. Supply Chain converts approved requisitions to
purchase orders, and goods are received against the purchase order before invoices are paid. Most
clinical supplies are delivered to the Stafford warehouse or directly to hospital docks.
No purchase may be committed verbally or by a supplier quote alone; a purchase order number is
required before delivery.
Blanket orders may be set up for recurring services, with releases issued against the blanket.
Receipts must be entered within two business days of delivery so that invoices can be matched.
4. Approval limits
Approval authority is based on the total value of the purchase order, including freight and
installation. Orders may not be split to stay under a limit.
Department director: up to $10,000.
Vice president: up to $100,000.
Chief Financial Officer: up to $500,000.
Chief Executive Officer: above $500,000.

5. Use of contracts
Where a group purchasing organization (GPO) agreement or a Tallowbrook local agreement covers
an item, the contracted item and price must be used. GPO agreements usually run three years.
Supply Chain negotiates local agreements where no GPO agreement fits.
Requests for an off-contract item must state why the contracted item is not suitable.
Sourcing managers review off-contract spend each quarter and identify items for contracting.
6. Value analysis
The Value Analysis Committee meets monthly and reviews requests for new products and
conversions between products. Requests with more than $25,000 in expected annual impact
require a clinical sponsor and a cost analysis prepared with Supply Chain.
The committee may approve, approve for a trial period, defer for more information or decline.
Trials must have a defined end date and evaluation criteria.
Decisions are recorded in the committee minutes and communicated by the Manager, Contracting
& Value Analysis.
7. Exceptions and emergencies
In an emergency affecting patient care or building safety, the house supervisor or administrator on
call may authorize an immediate purchase. A requisition must be entered on the next business day
and approved under Section 4.
8. Review
Supply Chain reviews this policy every two years or sooner if approval limits or systems change.
Questions should be directed to the Supply Chain office.

files.title: Clinical Engineering Program: Equipment Maintenance and AEM Procedure
files.filename: Clinical Engineering Program: Equipment Maintenance and AEM Procedure.docx
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 3.0
Clinical Engineering Program: 
Equipment Maintenance and AEM 
Procedure
Tallowbrook Health | Clinical Engineering | 2025-12-01 | v3.0
Procedure CE-01, version 3.0, effective December 1, 2025. Owner: Director, Clinical 
Engineering. Reviewed by the Environment of Care committee. Replaces version 2.2 (May 
2023).
1. Purpose and scope
This procedure describes how Clinical Engineering inventories, classifies, maintains and 
repairs medical equipment at Tallowbrook facilities, and how maintenance performance is 
measured and reported.
It applies to medical equipment at both hospitals, Outpatient Pavilion West, Imaging & 
Therapy Stafford and Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend. Surgery Center Grand Parkway 
devices are covered under its services agreement.
2. Organization
Clinical Engineering has 13 FTEs: a director, two senior specialists, nine technicians and a 
coordinator. Shops are located at Medical Center West and at the System Service Center in 
Stafford, which supports the Fort Bend sites.
Imaging equipment and medical lasers are serviced under manufacturer contracts. Clinical 
Engineering tracks these devices in inventory, schedules vendor visits and reviews vendor 
service reports.
3. Equipment inventory
Every medical device must pass an incoming inspection and be entered in the CMMS before 
clinical use. Inventory records are kept in two systems until consolidation:
 Legacy CE CMMS: Medical Center West and the Pavilion (in use since 2012).
 Enterprise CMMS: Hospital Fort Bend, the surgery center, Stafford and Mission Bend 
(since 2020). Facilities work orders are also in this system.
Tallowbrook Health • 3.0
4. Risk classification and critical equipment
Each device type is assigned high, medium or low risk based on its function, the 
consequence of failure and its maintenance requirements. The assignment is made by a 
senior specialist and recorded as a category default in the CMMS.
Critical equipment is equipment whose failure could result in serious injury or death to 
patients or staff. All critical equipment is classified high risk and is maintained according to 
the manufacturer's recommendations.
5. Maintenance strategies
Federal requirements allow a hospital to adjust maintenance activities and intervals from 
manufacturer recommendations, based on a documented risk assessment by qualified 
personnel.
Tallowbrook's alternate equipment maintenance (AEM) program applies this to eligible 
lower-risk devices.
 Manufacturer schedule required: imaging and radiologic equipment, medical lasers, 
new devices without sufficient maintenance history, and high-risk life-support devices.
 AEM eligible: other medium- and low-risk devices where the risk assessment supports a 
different interval or scope.
 AEM decisions are recorded by device category and reviewed at least annually, or 
sooner after an incident or recall.
6. Work order handling
Scheduled maintenance (PM), corrective repairs, incoming inspections and recall or alert 
actions are all recorded as work orders. The steps differ slightly between the two systems.
 Legacy CE CMMS: PM work orders are generated on the first of each month for the 
month. Requests for repair are phoned or emailed to the shop and entered by the 
coordinator.
 Enterprise CMMS: PM work orders are generated 14 days before the due date. Staff 
submit repair requests through the portal, which also routes facilities requests.
 In both systems a technician records labor hours, parts and the result, and closes the 
work order. A repair call where no fault is found is closed as the no problem found type.
7. Recalls and alerts
The coordinator reviews manufacturer and regulatory notices weekly, searches both 
systems for affected models and opens a recall or alert work order for each affected device. 
Unlocated devices are reported to the director within five business days.
Tallowbrook Health • 3.0
8. Performance measurement
Scheduled maintenance performance is the share of PM work orders completed by their due 
date. It is reported monthly to the Environment of Care committee overall, for high-risk 
devices and by CMMS instance.
The target is 95% overall and 100% for high-risk devices. Any overdue high-risk PM is 
escalated to the director the day it becomes overdue.

files.title: CMMS Consolidation — Business Case and Target Design
files.filename: CMMS Consolidation — Business Case and Target Design.docx
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 1.1
CMMS Consolidation — Business Case 
and Target Design
Tallowbrook Health | Clinical Engineering | 2026-06-10 | v1.1
Version 1.1, June 10, 2026. Prepared by Samuel Ibekwe, Director, Clinical Engineering, with 
Information Services. For decision by the executive team on June 24, 2026, and review by IS 
governance.
1. Summary and request
Clinical engineering equipment records are kept in two maintenance systems. This paper 
proposes moving all clinical engineering records into the enterprise CMMS already used by 
Facilities and by clinical engineering at the Fort Bend and outpatient sites.
We ask the executive team to approve the project and a one-time budget of $186,000, 
covering vendor configuration and temporary data-entry support. Data cleanup would run 
July to October 2026 and migration of legacy records January to April 2027.
2. Current state
The legacy CE CMMS has held Medical Center West and Pavilion records since 2012. The 
enterprise CMMS has held Hospital Fort Bend, surgery center, Stafford and Mission Bend 
records since 2020, along with all facilities work orders.
At the end of May 2026 about 1,660 clinical devices were on file: roughly 960 in the legacy 
system and 700 in the enterprise system. One team of 13 staff works across both.
3. Problems with two systems
 Different work order steps: legacy PM work orders are created monthly and repair 
requests arrive by phone or email; the enterprise CMMS creates PM work orders ahead 
of due dates and takes portal requests.
 Recalls and alerts must be searched in both systems, and model names are recorded 
differently in each.
 The EDW loads a weekly enterprise CMMS extract, but the legacy system is exported by 
hand once a month, so PM completion for the two Harris County sites lags by up to a 
month.
 Risk categories and AEM category defaults were set up separately and do not match for 
about 40 device types.
 The legacy system runs on an on-premise server that reaches end of vendor support in 
2027.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.1
4. Target design
All clinical engineering devices, work orders and history would be held in the enterprise 
CMMS. Clinical engineering would use its own work order types for scheduled maintenance, 
corrective repair, incoming inspection and recall or alert actions.
 One device type list and risk classification across all sites, with AEM decisions recorded 
against device types.
 Manufacturer schedules kept for imaging and radiologic equipment, lasers and new 
devices without maintenance history, which cannot be placed on alternate maintenance.
 PM completion loaded to the EDW for all sites through the existing weekly extract, using 
the standard measure: PM work orders completed by due date over PM work orders 
due.
 Open design questions for the requirements review: asset tag format, whether facilities 
and clinical engineering share one instance, and how risk levels are recorded.
5. Data cleanup and migration
July to October 2026: reconcile device types, fill missing model and serial numbers, retire 
records for devices no longer in service and align risk categories. A temporary data-entry 
specialist supports the coordinator.
January to April 2027: load legacy devices and five years of work order history, run both 
systems in parallel for one PM cycle, then set the legacy system to read-only.
6. Costs and benefits
One-time cost is estimated at $186,000. Retiring the legacy system avoids its annual 
maintenance fee and a server replacement. The main benefits are one process for 
technicians, timely reporting for all sites and a single search for recalls.
7. Risks
 Data quality in the legacy system is uneven; cleanup may take longer than planned.
 Technicians will carry both systems during parallel running.
 PM schedules must not slip during migration; high-risk PM stays at 100% on time 
throughout.

files.title: Operational Metric Definitions Standard
files.search:
Operational Metric Definitions Standard
Tallowbrook Health | Decision Support & Operational Reporting | 2025-02-01
Data Standard DS-02, version 3.0, effective February 1, 2025. Owner: Director, Decision Support &
Operational Reporting. Applies to all operational dashboards, the monthly operating review
package and department reports that use EDW data.
1. Purpose
This standard gives one definition for each operational metric used across Tallowbrook so that
dashboards, operating reviews and department reports produce the same numbers. Reports that
use a different definition must label it and explain the difference.
2. Data sources and timing
Metrics are calculated in the enterprise data warehouse (EDW) and published on the Pulse portal.
Most dashboards refresh nightly; staffing dashboards refresh after each pay period closes. Figures
for the most recent day or pay period may change after late documentation or pay corrections.
3. Inpatient capacity
Inpatient admissions: patients admitted to inpatient status. Observation stays are excluded,
including observation patients later converted, who count on the date of the inpatient order.
Patient days: inpatients counted at the midnight census.
Occupancy: midnight census divided by staffed beds. Facility occupancy in the operating review
uses inpatient patient days. Unit occupancy on bed management views also counts observation
patients in inpatient beds and therefore runs higher.
Average length of stay (ALOS): patient days divided by discharges for the same period.
Staffed beds: beds open and staffed under the approved staffing plan for the period, not licensed
beds.
4. Emergency department
ED visits: patients registered in the ED, including those who leave before being seen.
ED boarding hours: time from the inpatient admission order to the time the patient leaves the ED,
attributed to the destination unit. This definition has applied since February 2024; earlier reports
started the clock at the bed request.
5. Perioperative

Surgical cases: patients who entered an operating room for a scheduled or add-on procedure.
Procedure room cases are reported separately.
Block utilization: in-room to out-of-room minutes used within a service's block, divided by allocated
block minutes net of time released on schedule under the block policy.
6. Staffing
Planned RN hours: the official staffing grid applied to the actual census for each shift.
Variance: worked hours minus planned hours; positive values mean more hours were worked than
planned.
Overtime, float pool and agency percentages: each hour type divided by total worked hours.
7. Equipment maintenance
PM completion: scheduled maintenance work orders completed by their due date divided by
scheduled maintenance work orders due in the period. Reported overall, for high-risk devices and
by system, and reviewed monthly by the Environment of Care committee.
8. Use in the monthly operating review
The monthly operating review, held on the third Thursday, reports volumes, capacity, staffing,
quality and financial results by facility and service line using these definitions. Decision Support
prepares the package from the EDW after month-end close.
9. Changes to this standard
Requests to add or change a definition go to Decision Support. Changes take effect at the start of a
month and are recorded here. Version 3.0 adds the block utilization and PM completion definitions
and clarifies the treatment of observation patients.

files.title: Administrative Systems Landscape
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 2.0
Administrative Systems Landscape
Tallowbrook Health | Information Services | 2026-04-30 | v2.0
Architecture note, version 2.0, April 30, 2026. Prepared by Arjun Mehta, Vice President and 
Chief Information Officer, for Information Services, Decision Support and department 
system owners. Describes the administrative and operational systems in use, what each 
holds, how data moves between them and who owns them.
1. Scope
This note covers systems used to run operations: patient flow and scheduling, finance and 
purchasing, workforce, equipment and facilities maintenance, and operational reporting.
Clinical ancillary systems such as laboratory, pharmacy and imaging are mentioned only 
where they exchange data with these systems.
2. Enterprise EHR
The vendor-hosted EHR, implemented in 2019, supports admission, discharge and transfer 
(ADT), bed management, enterprise scheduling and clinical documentation.
It is used at both hospitals, Outpatient Pavilion West, Imaging & Therapy Stafford and 
Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend.
System owner: Information Services, with Nursing, Patient Access and Capacity 
Management as business owners for their modules.
3. ERP and supply systems
The ERP, live since FY2021, supports general ledger, purchasing, inventory, accounts 
payable and HR/payroll. Point-of-use supply cabinets in procedural and nursing areas 
record usage, which drives replenishment orders in the ERP.
Business owners: Finance for the general ledger and payables, Supply Chain for purchasing 
and inventory, Human Resources for payroll.
4. Workforce scheduling and timekeeping
The workforce scheduling and timekeeping system (WFS) holds staff schedules, time 
punches and premium pay codes. It sends worked hours to ERP payroll every pay period 
and scheduled and worked hours to the EDW nightly.
Business owners: Nursing Services and the Central Staffing Office.
Tallowbrook Health • 2.0
5. Maintenance systems
Clinical engineering records are split. The legacy CE CMMS, an on-premise system in use 
since 2012, holds Medical Center West and Pavilion devices.
The cloud enterprise CMMS holds facilities work orders for all sites and, since 2020, clinical 
engineering records for the other sites.
The legacy server reaches end of vendor support in 2027. Clinical Engineering and IS are 
assessing options, and any change will go to the architecture review board.
6. Surgery Center Grand Parkway
The surgery center is a joint venture with physician investors and schedules and bills cases 
in its own practice-management system, separate from the EHR.
It buys supply chain and clinical engineering services from Tallowbrook under a services 
agreement, so its purchases run through the ERP and its devices are in the enterprise 
CMMS.
7. Reporting and integration
The enterprise data warehouse (EDW) loads nightly between 1:00 and 5:30 a.m. and feeds 
the Pulse dashboard portal, which Decision Support maintains. Most dashboards refresh 
nightly; staffing dashboards refresh after each pay period closes.
An integration engine manages HL7 feeds between the EHR and ancillary systems and the 
flat-file transfers into the EDW.
8. Main data flows
Principal feeds into the EDW and payroll are shown below. Two feeds are not automated: 
the surgery center sends a monthly case summary file, and the legacy CE CMMS is exported 
by hand each month.
Tallowbrook Health • 2.0
9. Governance
The architecture review board, chaired by the CIO, meets monthly to review integration 
changes and new applications. Departments proposing a new system or interface submit a 
request to IS before selecting a vendor.

Tallowbrook Health • 1.4
EDW Nightly Loads and Interface 
Schedule
Tallowbrook Health | Decision Support & Operational Reporting | 2026-03-15  
| v1.4
Interface description, version 1.4, March 15, 2026. Owner: Priya Raman, Director, Decision 
Support & Operational Reporting, with the IS integration team. Lists each feed into the 
enterprise data warehouse (EDW), its timing and dependencies, and what happens when a 
load fails.
1. Load window
EDW loads run nightly between 1:00 and 5:30 a.m. Source extracts land first, 
transformations run next, and Pulse dashboards refresh at the end of the window so that 
figures are available when managers arrive.
File transfers are managed by the integration engine, which also handles HL7 feeds between 
the EHR and ancillary systems.
2. Feeds
 EHR ADT and bed management (nightly, 1:00 a.m.): admissions, transfers, discharges, 
midnight census, bed assignments and observation status for both hospitals.
 EHR ED and orders (nightly, 1:20 a.m.): ED arrivals, dispositions and admission order 
times used for boarding hours.
 EHR enterprise scheduling (nightly, 1:40 a.m.): templates, booked and completed 
appointments for the Pavilion, Stafford and Mission Bend, and surgical schedules for 
both hospitals.
 WFS (nightly, 2:30 a.m.): scheduled and worked hours by employee, cost center and pay 
code. Worked hours also go to ERP payroll each pay period.
 ERP (nightly, 3:00 a.m.): purchase orders, receipts, inventory issues and general ledger 
postings.
 Enterprise CMMS (weekly, Sunday 3:30 a.m.): assets and work orders for clinical 
engineering at the Fort Bend and outpatient sites, and facilities work orders for all sites.
 Legacy CE CMMS (monthly, manual): Clinical Engineering exports devices and work 
orders for Medical Center West and the Pavilion in the first week of the month; Decision 
Support loads the file.
 Surgery center case summary (monthly file): cases by service and room from the 
surgery center practice-management system, received by the tenth of the month.
Tallowbrook Health • 1.4
3. Dependencies
Census, boarding and discharge timing dashboards need both EHR feeds. Staffing 
dashboards use WFS data after each pay period closes, because late punches and 
corrections post during the following week.
 Equipment maintenance figures for Medical Center West and the Pavilion are up to a 
month behind other sites because of the manual export.
 Surgery center volumes appear in facility activity reports only after the monthly file 
arrives.
4. Failure handling
The integration engine alerts the on-call Decision Support analyst when an extract is late or 
fails validation. The analyst reruns the load by 7:00 a.m. where possible.
If a rerun is not possible, affected dashboards show the prior day's data with a banner, and 
the analyst notifies report owners by email.
 Row-count checks compare each feed with the prior seven days and flag changes over 
20%.
 Failed loads and reruns are logged in the Decision Support operations log.
5. Change control
New feeds or changes to timing are requested through IS and reviewed by the architecture 
review board before build. Version 1.4 moves the WFS extract from 4:00 to 2:30 a.m. so that 
staffing views refresh before the 5 a.m. staffing huddle.

files.title: Hospital Fort Bend Fourth Floor: Options for the FY2028 Capital Plan
files.filename: Hospital Fort Bend Fourth Floor: Options for the FY2028 Capital Plan.docx
files.search:
Tallowbrook Health • 0.9 (draft for executive review)
Hospital Fort Bend Fourth Floor: 
Options for the FY2028 Capital Plan
Tallowbrook Health | Office of the President, Hospital Fort Bend | 2026-09-
12 | v0.9 (draft for executive review)
Decision memo, draft for executive review, September 12, 2026. From Janelle Brooks, 
President, Tallowbrook Hospital Fort Bend, with Strategy & Communications and Facilities 
& Plant Operations. To the executive team.
Request
Approve $350,000 for schematic design covering both build-out scopes described below, so 
that cost estimates can be refined before the board decides on the fourth floor in February 
2027 as part of the FY2028 capital plan.
This memo does not recommend an option. It sets out the evidence and the choices so the 
executive team can decide what to take to the board.
The hospital today
Hospital Fort Bend has 112 licensed beds, of which 96 are staffed, a 24-hour emergency 
department with 24 treatment spaces and six operating rooms. The fourth floor was built as 
shell space sized for 36 beds.
Obstetric patients are referred to Medical Center West, where Women's & Infant Services is 
offered. None of the options below adds obstetrics.
 ICU: 12 beds
 2 North Medical-Surgical: 32 beds
 3 North Medical-Surgical/Telemetry: 30 beds
 3 South Surgical: 22 beds
Demand
FY2026 admissions were 5,893, up 7.2% on FY2025, with 24,616 patient days and an 
average length of stay of 4.18 days. Average occupancy of staffed beds rose from 66.0% to 
70.3%.
ED visits rose 5.6% to 43,112, and the hospital performed 4,589 surgical cases.
Growth has continued. In July and August 2026 admissions were 1,006 against 948 a year 
earlier, and ED visits 7,677 against 7,254.
Tallowbrook Health • 0.9 (draft for executive review)
Where the pressure is
Average occupancy understates pressure on the medical units. From February to August 
2026, midnight occupancy including observation patients was 76.4% for the hospital, above 
Medical Center West at 75.6%.
 2 North: 81.8%
 3 North: 80.5%
 ICU: 73.2%
 3 South: 64.6%
Market outlook
Planning assumes continued population and household growth in the Fort Bend service 
area.
The strategy team refreshes demand projections each fall before the capital plan; this year's 
refresh was completed in August and will be updated again before the board meeting.
Options
Preliminary estimates are order of magnitude and will change with design.
 A. Defer. No capital in FY2028; manage growth through length of stay, flow work and 
use of 3 South capacity.
 B. Build 18 medical-surgical beds as phase 1 in FY2028. Preliminary estimate $14.5 
million (about $0.81 million per bed); the remaining shell stays available.
 C. Build all 36 beds in FY2028. Preliminary estimate $26.0 million (about $0.72 million 
per bed).
Considerations
 Option A carries the risk that the medical units run above 80% more often as volumes 
grow, increasing ED boarding at Fort Bend.
 Option B costs more per bed and needs a second construction period on an occupied 
floor later.
 Option C gives the lowest cost per bed but adds staffing and operating costs before 
demand may need all 36 beds.
 3 South ran at 64.6%; any option should be tested against using some surgical beds for 
medical patients.
 New beds must be staffed. Central Staffing float pool growth at Fort Bend should be 
reflected in the staffing plan for any build-out.
Tallowbrook Health • 0.9 (draft for executive review)
Next steps
If design funding is approved, schematic design would run October to December 2026, with 
refined estimates and updated demand projections in January 2027 ahead of the February 
board meeting.

About Tallowbrook Health
Tallowbrook Health (Tallowbrook Community Health System) is a Texas nonprofit, tax-exempt
regional health system based in west Houston. It operates two community hospitals, Medical
Center West in Harris County and Hospital Fort Bend in Richmond, and four outpatient facilities in
Harris and Fort Bend counties: Outpatient Pavilion West, Surgery Center Grand Parkway, Imaging
& Therapy Stafford and Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend.
Why we assess community needs
Federal tax rules require nonprofit hospitals to conduct a community health needs assessment
(CHNA) every three years and adopt a strategy to address the needs identified. Tallowbrook's
board adopted its 2025 CHNA in June 2025 and this implementation strategy in November 2025.
Priorities for FY2026 to FY2028
The assessment drew on public health data for Harris and Fort Bend counties, community surveys
and discussions with local organizations. Tallowbrook will focus on three priorities:
Access to primary care, especially for residents without a regular source of care.
Chronic disease management, with an emphasis on diabetes.
Maternal health, including prenatal care and support after delivery.
Programs
ED navigation: patients seen in Tallowbrook emergency departments who have no regular provider
are offered help to establish primary care.
Transportation vouchers for residents who would otherwise miss primary care, prenatal or diabetes
education visits.
Diabetes education classes at Urgent & Family Care Mission Bend, which also offers primary care
with six providers, urgent care from 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, X-ray and a lab draw station.
Prenatal education and postpartum follow-up calls through Women's & Infant Services at Medical
Center West.

How we will measure progress
Tallowbrook will report each year on aggregate program measures, not on individual patients:
Number of ED navigation referrals and the share that result in a completed primary care visit.
Transportation vouchers issued and visits completed.
Diabetes education class sessions and participants.
Postpartum follow-up calls completed.
Needs not directly addressed
The assessment also identified housing, behavioral health services and food access. Tallowbrook
is not the lead organization for these needs and will support partners through referrals and
participation in county coalitions rather than through its own programs.
Contact
Questions and comments on the CHNA or this strategy are welcome and will be considered in the
next assessment. Contact Tallowbrook Community Health through the system office in west
Houston.

2026 Hurricane Season Readiness Summary
Tallowbrook Health | Facilities & Plant Operations | 2026-06-01
Readiness memo to the emergency management committee and facility leaders, June 1, 2026.
Prepared by Wesley Tran, Emergency Management Coordinator, with Facilities & Plant Operations.
Confirms readiness actions for the season running June 1 to November 30.
Summary
The four standing readiness actions for hurricane season are complete or scheduled for all six
facilities and the System Service Center: generator load tests, a review of 96-hour supply par
levels, ride-out team rosters and a review of patient transfer agreements. Two items remain open
and are listed below with owners and dates.
Generator load tests
Owner: Kenneth Duhon, Director, Facilities & Plant Operations.
Medical Center West and Hospital Fort Bend: full-load tests completed in May; fuel tanks topped off
and fuel delivery contracts confirmed.
Outpatient Pavilion West and Imaging & Therapy Stafford: tests completed in May.
System Service Center: test completed; transfer switch repair scheduled for June 12 (open item).
96-hour supply par levels
Owner: Supply Chain. Par levels for medical-surgical supplies, linen, food and water were reviewed
against a 96-hour stand-alone period for both hospitals. The Stafford warehouse at the System
Service Center holds the surge stock and will pre-position supplies at both hospitals when a storm
is forecast to reach the area within 72 hours.
Ride-out team rosters
Owners: hospital chief nursing officers and department directors.
Team A (ride-out) and Team B (relief) rosters confirmed for both hospitals for June; rosters are
refreshed monthly through November.
Clinical Engineering, Facilities and Information Services on-site staff included in the hospital
rosters.
Central scheduling call center at the System Service Center will move to remote operation if the
building closes.

Patient transfer agreements
Owner: Emergency Management Coordinator. Transfer agreements with receiving hospitals
outside the coastal area were reviewed; one agreement is being renewed and is expected to be
signed by June 30 (open item). Outpatient sites and Surgery Center Grand Parkway will close to
scheduled patients ahead of a forecast landfall according to their site plans.
Open items
System Service Center transfer switch repair: Facilities, June 12.
Renewal of one patient transfer agreement: Emergency Management, June 30.
Next review
The emergency management committee will review readiness again on August 1, at the start of
peak season, and after any activation.
