files.filename: Contractor Management and Field Safety Requirements.pdf
files.search:
Contractor Management and Field Safety
 Requirements
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Contractor Management with Safety, Health and Environment |
2026-02-02
These requirements apply to every contractor working for Sedgewater Electric Delivery or
Sedgewater Gas Distribution under a master service agreement. They cover prequalification,
releases and approvals, field audits, safety rules and storm work. Issued by Contractor
Management on February 2, 2026; shared with contractor safety leads.
1. Who this applies to
Sedgewater has 34 contractors under master service agreements covering line construction,
underground and boring, pole inspection, vegetation, gas construction, locating, traffic control and
contact overflow. Subcontractors must meet the same requirements and be named on the release.
2. Prequalification
Each contractor holds one of three statuses. Approved contractors may receive releases in their
scope. 'Approved - conditional' means a corrective safety plan is in place; releases continue but
audits increase. Suspended contractors may not receive new releases, and their open work is
reassigned.
Rate tiers A, B and C reflect scope size and audit history. Pinehaven Line Services has been
conditionally approved since February 2026 with a corrective safety plan.
3. Releases and approvals
All work is authorized through a release that sets the contractor, program, district, funding and
authorized value. Work orders must reference an active release.
Release approval limits: district managers up to $250,000; directors up to $2 million; vice presidents
up to $10 million; the COO above $10 million.
4. Field safety audits
Sedgewater audits contractor crews in the field at least monthly for tier A contractors and quarterly
for tier B and C, and weekly while a contractor is conditionally approved. Audits are recorded on
form SHE-F-112 revision B and shared with the contractor's safety lead within five working days.
5. Safety rules
Line work follows OSHA 1910.269 for the operation and maintenance of transmission and
distribution lines and equipment. Contractors report every recordable injury, DART case, vehicle
incident and high-potential near miss to Sedgewater within 24 hours. The 2026 employee TRIR

target of 1.40 is also the benchmark used in contractor performance reviews.
6. Storm work
During activations contractors follow Sedgewater's restoration priorities: public safety hazards first,
then registered critical facilities, substations and main feeders, laterals and individual services.
Storm releases are issued by storm command and close when crews are released.
7. Workforce
Qualified line workers are scarce: about 131,900 people held power-line installer and repairer jobs
in the United States in 2025, with median pay of $95,320 in May 2025, and about half work for
utilities. Contractors must keep crew rosters current so that storm command can plan capacity.

files.title: Gas Leak Management Procedure
files.search:
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 5.0
Gas Leak Management Procedure
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Gas Compliance and Integrity | 2026-04-06 | 
v5.0
This procedure sets how Sedgewater Gas Distribution finds, grades, repairs and monitors 
gas leaks and how leak survey work is scheduled. It covers the three gas districts, 
Crossroads, Bayou and Prairie. Issued by Gas Compliance on April 6, 2026.
1. Scope
The procedure covers mains, services, meter sets and regulator stations serving the 
262,300 customers counted at December 31, 2025 (Crossroads 96,400, Bayou 117,800, 
Prairie 48,100).
2. How leaks are found
Leaks are found by scheduled leak surveys, customer odor calls, crews working on the 
system and third-party reports. Gas odor and emergency calls are handled by the contact 
center as priority calls and dispatched to a service technician without delay; customers are 
told to leave the building and call from outside.
3. Leak grades
 Grade 1 - a hazard that needs immediate repair or continuous action until the hazard is 
removed.
 Grade 2 - non-hazardous at detection but scheduled for repair.
 Grade 3 - non-hazardous and monitored at each survey until repaired or cleared.
4. Repair and monitoring
The first technician on site grades the leak, makes the area safe and records the leak in the 
leak log. Grade 1 leaks stay under continuous action until the hazard is removed. Grade 2 
repairs are scheduled by the district gas supervisor; Appendix A lists repair timeframes by 
grade. Grade 3 leaks are rechecked at each survey and upgraded if readings rise.
5. Leak survey intervals
Federal rules require leak surveys in business districts at intervals not exceeding 15 months 
and at least once each calendar year. Outside business districts, surveys are required at 
least once every five calendar years at intervals not exceeding 63 months, with shorter 
intervals for certain cathodically unprotected lines.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 5.0
Sedgewater surveys business districts every year, unprotected steel areas every three years 
and all other areas every five years.
6. Unprotected steel
At the end of 2025 the system had 84 miles of unprotected steel main. Leaks on unprotected 
steel are repaired by replacement where practical, and the areas are resurveyed every three 
years until the steel is retired. The replacement program aims to remove all unprotected 
steel main by the end of 2029.
7. Records and reporting
Leak records feed the distribution integrity management program, which must consider 
corrosion, natural forces, excavation damage, other outside force, material or weld failure, 
equipment failure and incorrect operations. Operators submit facilities-replacement 
documentation and work plans to the RRC by March 15; the 2026 submission was made on 
March 11. The PHMSA annual report for the preceding year is also due by March 15.
Appendix A. Repair timeframes
Grade 1: immediate and continuous action. Grade 2: see current rule. Grade 3: re-evaluate at 
each scheduled survey.

(DIMP) for 2026: system inventory, leak history, threat ranking and additional measures. Prepared

Relative to main mileage, unprotected steel had about 243 non-excavation leaks per 100 miles of
main, protected steel 75 and polyethylene 20. The rate uses all leaks on mains and services divided
by main miles.
4. 2026 threat ranking
1. Excavation damage.
2. Corrosion on unprotected steel (roughly 85 miles of main).
3. Material, weld and joint failures in early plastics and older fittings.
4. Natural forces, mainly flooding and soil movement.
5. Equipment failure at regulators and meters.
5. Additional measures
Sedgewater is accelerating unprotected steel replacement, with the aim of removing it by the end of
2029; the 2026 target is 22 miles of main and 2,400 steel services. Remaining unprotected lines are
surveyed every three years. Excavator outreach is concentrated in high-growth Crossroads areas,
and crews inspect exposed facilities after major rain events.
The 4 miles of other plastic main have few leaks in absolute terms, but the sample is too small to
compare leak rates reliably, so the ranking treats early plastics together with older fittings.
6. Leak surveys
Business districts are surveyed every year, unprotected steel areas every three years and all other
areas every five years. Outside business districts the federal minimum is once every five calendar
years at intervals not exceeding 63 months.
7. Submissions

Operators submit facilities-replacement documentation and work plans to the RRC by March 15,
and each distribution operator submits a PHMSA annual report by March 15 for the preceding year.
The 2026 RRC submission was made on March 11 and the 2025 PHMSA annual report on March

Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.3
Operational Systems Landscape and 
Data Flows
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | IT and OT Enterprise Architecture | 2026-05-
15 | v1.3
This document describes the operational business systems used by Sedgewater's electric 
and gas delivery businesses, the main data flows between them and the extracts used for 
reporting. It is maintained by the Enterprise Architect and reflects the landscape at May 15, 
2026.
1. Scope
The landscape covers systems that hold work, outage, meter, asset, customer, market and 
financial records. Distribution control and substation automation systems are managed 
separately by IT and OT and are outside the scope of this document.
2. Core systems
 Work management system (WMS), version 8, installed 2017: work orders, scheduling 
and crew time.
 Outage management system (OMS), 2019: outage prediction, crew dispatch and 
interruption records.
 Meter data management (MDM), 2012, upgraded 2021: interval data, meter events and 
remote service-order execution.
 Geographic information system (GIS), 2015: network model and asset records.
 Enterprise resource planning (ERP), 2020: finance, projects, procurement and 
inventory.
 Gas customer information and billing system, 2016.
 Market transaction gateway: TX SET transactions with ERCOT and REPs.
 Cloud contact center platform, 2023: telephony, IVR, text and web channels.
3. Main data flows
The GIS network model feeds OMS; meter outage events flow from MDM to OMS; completed 
work orders send labor and material costs from WMS to ERP; service-order results flow 
from MDM to the market gateway. Nightly extracts from WMS, OMS and ERP load the 
reporting database used for management reports and regulatory filings.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.3
4. Interruption records
OMS is the system of record for sustained interruptions. Rules require records showing 
type, cause, date and time, duration, customers affected and substation and feeder 
identifiers, kept for five years. Reliability indices are calculated from OMS extracts under the 
Reliability Metric Definitions and Calculation Standard.
5. Market transactions
REPs submit service orders through the market transaction gateway, and most are 
completed remotely through the meter network. TX SET 814 transactions cover 
enrollments, switches, move-ins, move-outs and ESI ID maintenance; 867 transactions carry 
usage. Final usage (867_03) goes from Sedgewater to ERCOT within three business days of 
the meter read.
6. Meters and customer channels
The current advanced meter fleet was installed from 2011 to 2013, and vendor support for 
this meter generation ends in 2030. One contact center at the Houston operations center 
handles electric and gas contacts, with an overflow partner for storms and billing peaks; 
customers can also report outages by text, web and automated phone.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.3
7. Known data gaps
Streetlight repairs are logged in WMS without a feeder code because the lighting network is 
recorded separately in GIS, so streetlight work cannot be joined to feeder-level reports.

files.title: Retail Electric Provider Service Guide
files.search:
Retail Electric Provider Service Guide
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Customer and Market Operations | 2026-06-01
This guide explains how retail electric providers (REPs) work with Sedgewater Electric Delivery:
what Sedgewater does and does not do, how service orders and usage flow, how outages are
reported and whom to contact. It is published for REPs operating in the Sedgewater service area.
Edition of June 1, 2026.
1. Our role
Sedgewater Electric Delivery is a transmission and distribution service provider (TDSP) in the
ERCOT region. It builds, operates and maintains poles, wires, substations and meters, restores
outages and processes service orders. It does not generate electricity or sell it to end-use
customers.
In ERCOT, a TDSP owns or operates transmission or distribution facilities for compensation, is
regulated by the PUCT, must provide non-discriminatory access and registers with ERCOT. The
rates TDSPs charge are set by the PUCT.
2. Customers, REPs and charges
58 REPs are active in the service area. REPs bill end-use customers and pay Sedgewater its
regulated delivery charges; Sedgewater invoices REPs each business day. A TDSP's delivery
charge can include base transmission and distribution rates, DCRF, TCRF, energy-efficiency and
securitization charges.
Residential and small commercial distribution rates are mainly energy-based, most large
commercial and industrial rates are based on peak demand, and every REP pays the same rates.
3. Service orders
REPs submit move-ins, move-outs, switches, disconnects and reconnects for non-payment,
re-reads and investigations through the market transaction gateway. Most are completed remotely
through the meter network. TX SET 814 transactions carry enrollments, switches, move-ins and
move-outs; 867 transactions carry usage.
Sedgewater returns a service-order response within one retail business day when it rejects an order
or cannot complete it. In 2025 REPs submitted 1,179,882 service orders; 98.7% of completed
orders were completed by the requested date and 91% were completed remotely.
4. Usage and invoices
Final usage (867_03) goes to ERCOT within three business days of the meter read. The usage
transaction and the TDSP invoice (810_02) are usually paired to trigger the REP's customer billing.

5. Outages and hazards
Customers should report outages and hazards to Sedgewater, not to their REP. Each REP chooses
how customer outage calls reach Sedgewater: by transaction, by forwarding calls, or by giving
customers the Sedgewater outage number. Sedgewater's electric contacts cover outages, hazards,
meter access, streetlights and service-order questions; billing questions go to the REP.
6. Critical care and critical load
REPs requesting disconnection of critical load or critical care customers must coordinate with
Sedgewater before the order is worked.
7. Storms and system outages
During Level 1 and Level 2 storm activations Sedgewater issues a REP bulletin at every restoration
update. Market procedures also cover extended unplanned market-system outages; Sedgewater
sends market notices for its own system outages.
8. Contacts
Market Operations help desk: weekdays 7 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Monthly REP forum: second Tuesday of each month.
Construction and new-service escalations: newservice-escalations@ (mailbox to be assigned).

rows: Feeder Register and 2026 Pole Inspection Results
Provide the feeder register snapshot and all 2026 inspection batches to date.
See each dataset dictionary and summary. Missing numeric values are excluded, not zero.
Descriptive statistics of selected records only. Totals of percentages and adjustment values are not operating KPIs.

Workbook of the distribution feeder register at August 31, 2026 and the pole inspection batches closed from January to August 2026. Prepared by the Pole Program for asset planning and for the draft pole management plan.

Data 1 - feeder register: one row per in-service feeder with district, substation code, customers, overhead and underground circuit miles, voltage class, decade in service, automation, resiliency scope, last cycle trim, 2025 worst-feeder flag and pole count.
Data 2 - pole inspection batches: one row per feeder section inspected by one contractor in one month, with outcomes and the number of poles installed before 1980.
Summary - formula totals of each numeric column.

The register lists 436 feeders from 102 substations with 8,860 overhead and 5,400 underground circuit miles (38% underground). Automation: 162 feeders with reclosers only, 134 with none, 102 with IGSD loops and 38 with full automation. The 2025 worst-feeder flag marks the 32 feeders on the 2025 list.
Sedgewater owns about 290,400 distribution poles, about 94% of them wood. Last cycle trim dates follow the four-year vegetation cycle.
Poles are inspected on a ten-year cycle, about 29,000 a year; the 2026 plan calls for 29,500 inspections. The 2026 cycle area is mainly Bayou, plus hardening-scope feeders in Harbor and Prairie.

January to August: 19,650 poles inspected, 18,392 passed (93.6%), 413 restorable by bracing or reinforcement, 177 priority rejects and 668 standard rejects (4.3% rejected). 83% of the poles inspected were installed before 1980.
Harbor 2,785 inspected, 4.3% rejected; Crossroads 292 inspected, 6.8% rejected; Bayou 14,056 inspected, 4.1% rejected; Prairie 2,517 inspected, 5.2% rejected.

Pass; restorable (bracing or reinforcement); priority reject (replace within 90 days); standard reject (replace within 12 months). Batches record counts only; pole identifiers and locations are held in GIS.
Last cycle trim is blank for the four all-underground feeders.

Field Work Orders and 
Crew Hours: Bayou and 
Crossroads Districts, 
January-August 2026
Workbook of field work orders created from January to August 2026 in the Bayou and Crossroads districts, with 
weekly crew hours for all four districts. Extracted from the work management system on September 9, 2026 for the 
operations review.
Data 1 - work orders: one row per order with district, feeder, type, priority, created, scheduled and completed dates, 
crew type, contractor, labor hours, material cost, status and storm flag.
Work orders cover Bayou and Crossroads only, the two districts that moved to the current WMS configuration first; 
crew capacity covers all four districts. Remotely completed service orders and storm restoration tickets are not work 
orders and are not included.
9,600 orders were created from January to August: 8,911 completed, 352 scheduled, 216 cancelled, 87 awaiting 
material and 34 awaiting a planned outage. The 87 awaiting material are 71 transformer replacements, 9 pole 
replacements and 7 small new services.
Median calendar days from creation to completion: P1 emergency 0 days (1,711 completed); P2 same day 0 days 
(2,518); P3 within 10 days 7 days (3,026); P4 planned 34 days (1,656). Recorded labor was 41,185 hours and material 
$8.3 million; 102 orders were storm-related.
In the 35 weeks to August 31, crews logged 1,008,195 regular and 112,359 overtime hours (overtime 10.0% of 
worked hours) against 1,074,645 available hours. 61,717 hours were charged to storms, 42,588 of them in the two 
weeks from May 18. Overtime share by district: Harbor 9.8%, Crossroads 10.2%, Bayou 9.9%, Prairie 10.2%.
Priorities: P1 emergency (respond immediately), P2 same day, P3 within 10 calendar days, P4 planned. Statuses: 
Scheduled, Completed, Cancelled, 'Open - awaiting material' and 'Open - awaiting outage'; an order is set to an 
awaiting status only after the planner confirms the constraint. Crew types: internal line, troubleman, underground, 
contract line and contract vegetation.
Data notes 562 orders (5.9%) have no feeder code; all are streetlight work, which is logged without a feeder because the lighting 
network is recorded separately in GIS. Since March 2026 internal troubleman crews have handled streetlight repairs 
that previously went to the lighting contractor.

sheets.name: Read me
rows: Field Work Orders and Crew Hours: Bayou and Crossroads Districts, January-August 2026
Provide work orders and weekly crew-hours for two districts to show workload, priorities and capacity.
See each dataset dictionary and summary. Missing numeric values are excluded, not zero.
Descriptive statistics of selected records only. Totals of percentages and adjustment values are not operating KPIs.

Workbook of field work orders created from January to August 2026 in the Bayou and Crossroads districts, with weekly crew hours for all four districts. Extracted from the work management system on September 9, 2026 for the operations review.
Data 1 - work orders: one row per order with district, feeder, type, priority, created, scheduled and completed dates, crew type, contractor, labor hours, material cost, status and storm flag.
Data 2 - crew capacity: available, regular, overtime and storm hours by district, crew type and week.
Summary - formula totals of each numeric column.

Work orders cover Bayou and Crossroads only, the two districts that moved to the current WMS configuration first; crew capacity covers all four districts. Remotely completed service orders and storm restoration tickets are not work orders and are not included.

9,600 orders were created from January to August: 8,911 completed, 352 scheduled, 216 cancelled, 87 awaiting material and 34 awaiting a planned outage. The 87 awaiting material are 71 transformer replacements, 9 pole replacements and 7 small new services.

Median calendar days from creation to completion: P1 emergency 0 days (1,711 completed); P2 same day 0 days (2,518); P3 within 10 days 7 days (3,026); P4 planned 34 days (1,656). Recorded labor was 41,185 hours and material $8.3 million; 102 orders were storm-related.

In the 35 weeks to August 31, crews logged 1,008,195 regular and 112,359 overtime hours (overtime 10.0% of worked hours) against 1,074,645 available hours. 61,717 hours were charged to storms, 42,588 of them in the two weeks from May 18. Overtime share by district: Harbor 9.8%, Crossroads 10.2%, Bayou 9.9%, Prairie 10.2%.

Priorities: P1 emergency (respond immediately), P2 same day, P3 within 10 calendar days, P4 planned. Statuses: Scheduled, Completed, Cancelled, 'Open - awaiting material' and 'Open - awaiting outage'; an order is set to an awaiting status only after the planner confirms the constraint. Crew types: internal line, troubleman, underground, contract line and contract vegetation.

562 orders (5.9%) have no feeder code; all are streetlight work, which is logged without a feeder because the lighting network is recorded separately in GIS. Since March 2026 internal troubleman crews have handled streetlight repairs that previously went to the lighting contractor.

Sustained Interruption 
Events, January 2025 - 
August 2026
Workbook of sustained interruption events from January 2025 to August 2026, extracted from the outage 
management system on September 9, 2026 by Reliability Engineering. Each row is one sustained interruption at 
transformer-fuse level or above.
Every event is classified as forced, planned, outside cause or major event. Planned interruptions have at least 24 
hours' notice; outside-cause interruptions start on the transmission grid or at a customer facility; momentary 
interruptions of five minutes or less are not in the extract. Headline indices under the Reliability Metric Definitions 
and Calculation Standard use forced events only and the average of monthly delivery points.
Records carry type, cause, date and start hour, duration, customers interrupted and feeder identifiers, as the 
interruption record rule requires.
2025, excluding major events: SAIDI 118.0 minutes, SAIFI 1.210, CAIDI 97.5 minutes from 4,560 forced interruptions. 
January to August 2026: SAIDI 84.0 minutes and SAIFI 0.830, against 83.3 minutes and 0.850 for January to August 
2025.
June 11-13, 2025: 355 interruptions, 104,000 customers, 126.4 million customer minutes. May 19-22, 2026: 463 
interruptions, 132,152 customers, 116.6 million customer minutes. Both met the major-event test and are flagged in 
the major event column.
In 2025, vegetation caused 26% of forced customer minutes, overhead equipment 22%, underground equipment 
16%, lightning 10%, animals 10%, wind 9%, vehicles or public 4% and unknown 3%.
Cause is coded Unknown for about 4% of events; crews are asked to update it when the repair is closed. Customer 
minutes equal customers interrupted multiplied by duration for every row.

Capital project register for 2026 with monthly actual spend by project from January to August, prepared by Capital 
Portfolio after the August close. Budget, forecast and in-service dates reflect the September 2026 forecast.
Data 1 - project register: 2026 budget, forecast and actual to date, total budget, program, business, district, stage, 
sponsor and planned and forecast in-service dates.
The 2026 capital budget is $1,120 million across 152 projects. January to August actual spend was $683.0 million 
(61% of budget) and the September forecast is $1,108 million.
By business (budget / actual / forecast): Electric $930 million / $570.4 million / $920 million; Gas $150 million / $92.8 
million / $150 million; Shared $40 million / $19.8 million / $38 million. Monthly spend rose from $68.6 million in 
January to $109.6 million in August.
Growth - new service $248 million; Transmission $142 million; Growth - substation and feeder $131 million; 
Reliability - distribution $118 million; Gas - pipe replacement $78 million; Resiliency - pole replacement $62 million.
Resiliency programs have a 2026 budget of $196 million; $109.0 million was spent to August and the forecast is $180 
million, mainly because strategic undergrounding is forecast at $26 million against a $42 million budget.
37 of 152 projects forecast in-service dates later than planned; 5 of them are undergrounding projects. Two 
undergrounding projects show forecast in-service dates earlier than baseline after their scope was reduced in July 
2026.
CP-26-050 Harbor North 138 kV substation and feeders (Design): $6.5 million in 2026 for design and long-lead 
equipment of an estimated $85 million; planned in service December 15, 2028.
CP-26-085 Next-generation meter pilot (Construct): $14.8 million in 2026 of a $16.5 million total; forecast in service 
moved from December 18, 2026 to January 29, 2027.
Projects move through Initiate, Design, Construct, In service and Closeout. Projects above $50 million need board 
approval.

sheets.name: Read me
rows: Capital Project Register and Monthly Spend, 2026
List every 2026 capital project with budget, forecast, actual and in-service dates, plus monthly actuals.
See each dataset dictionary and summary. Missing numeric values are excluded, not zero.
Descriptive statistics of selected records only. Totals of percentages and adjustment values are not operating KPIs.

Capital project register for 2026 with monthly actual spend by project from January to August, prepared by Capital Portfolio after the August close. Budget, forecast and in-service dates reflect the September 2026 forecast.
Data 1 - project register: 2026 budget, forecast and actual to date, total budget, program, business, district, stage, sponsor and planned and forecast in-service dates.
Data 2 - monthly actuals by project, January to August 2026.
Summary - formula totals of each numeric column.
The 2026 capital budget is $1,120 million across 152 projects. January to August actual spend was $683.0 million (61% of budget) and the September forecast is $1,108 million.

By business (budget / actual / forecast): Electric $930 million / $570.4 million / $920 million; Gas $150 million / $92.8 million / $150 million; Shared $40 million / $19.8 million / $38 million. Monthly spend rose from $68.6 million in January to $109.6 million in August.

Growth - new service $248 million; Transmission $142 million; Growth - substation and feeder $131 million; Reliability - distribution $118 million; Gas - pipe replacement $78 million; Resiliency - pole replacement $62 million.

Resiliency programs have a 2026 budget of $196 million; $109.0 million was spent to August and the forecast is $180 million, mainly because strategic undergrounding is forecast at $26 million against a $42 million budget.

37 of 152 projects forecast in-service dates later than planned; 5 of them are undergrounding projects. Two undergrounding projects show forecast in-service dates earlier than baseline after their scope was reduced in July 2026.
CP-26-050 Harbor North 138 kV substation and feeders (Design): $6.5 million in 2026 for design and long-lead equipment of an estimated $85 million; planned in service December 15, 2028.
CP-26-085 Next-generation meter pilot (Construct): $14.8 million in 2026 of a $16.5 million total; forecast in service moved from December 18, 2026 to January 29, 2027.
CP-26-096 Work management system upgrade, phase 0 (Initiate): $1.2 million in 2026.
Projects move through Initiate, Design, Construct, In service and Closeout. Projects above $50 million need board approval.

including all 70 business-district areas, and no area was past its due date.
Business districts are surveyed every year, unprotected steel areas every three years and other areas every five 
years. Federal rules require business-district surveys at intervals not exceeding 15 months and at least once each 
calendar year, and other areas at least once every five calendar years at intervals not exceeding 63 months.

files.title: May 19-22, 2026 Wind Event: After-Action Review
files.search:
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
May 19-22, 2026 Wind Event: After-
Action Review
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Emergency Preparedness and Resiliency | 
2026-07-24 | v1.0
After-action review of the May 19-22, 2026 wind event, prepared by Emergency 
Preparedness and Resiliency with the four district managers. It records what happened, 
how restoration went, what customers experienced and the actions agreed. Figures are 
from the outage management system, the restoration log and the contact center platform; 
cost figures are estimates at July 10, 2026.
1. Event summary
On the afternoon of May 19, 2026 a line of severe thunderstorms with straight-line winds 
crossed the service area, with the heaviest damage in Bayou and Prairie. A second band of 
storms on the night of May 20 caused further lateral and service outages.
The event produced 463 sustained interruptions affecting 132,152 customers in total and 
116.6 million customer minutes. It met the major-event test: loss of power to 10% or more 
of customers in a region over 24 hours, with not all restored within 24 hours.
2. Where customers lost power
Customers interrupted by district: Harbor 13,194, Crossroads 23,784, Bayou 55,484 and 
Prairie 39,690.
3. Restoration progress
Customers out peaked at 96,400 at 18:00 on May 19. Of the 132,152 affected customers, 
60% were restored by noon on May 20, 94% by 06:00 on May 21 and 99.6% by midnight on 
May 21. The last customers were restored by 18:00 on May 22.
The second band of storms on May 20 slowed progress in Bayou and Prairie, where crews 
returned to laterals they had already restored.
4. Damage
Field assessment recorded 1,140 broken poles, 2,380 spans of wire down and 610 failed 
transformers.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
5. Resources and mutual assistance
Field resources peaked at 424 crews at 06:00 on May 20: 82 internal line, 90 contract line, 
78 mutual-assistance and 174 vegetation crews.
Sedgewater requested mutual assistance through its regional group on the evening of May 
19. The first mutual-assistance crews began work on the morning of May 20 and the last 
were released on May 23. Mutual assistance is a voluntary partnership that shares crews, 
equipment and materials under standing agreements.
6. Priorities and critical facilities
Crews followed the restoration priorities: public safety hazards first, then registered critical 
facilities, substations and main feeders, laterals and individual services. Four leased mobile 
generation units (6.4 MW in total) supplied two public water facilities and one hospital 
campus, each for less than 30 hours.
7. Customer contact
Electric contacts reached 205,440 in May against 49,645 in April. Outage reports made up 
161,557 of them, and 78% of outage reports were completed by text, web or automated 
phone without an agent.
The overflow contact partner was activated on the evening of May 19 with 120 agents and 
stood down on May 25. Even so, electric average speed of answer was 175 seconds for the 
month and reached 11 minutes 40 seconds on May 20, against a storm target of under three 
minutes; 12.1% of queued electric calls were abandoned.
8. Estimated restoration times
Area-level estimated restoration times were published for each district every six hours from 
May 20. Premise-level estimates shown to customers were not stored after the event, so 
their accuracy cannot be measured. This review therefore assesses only the area estimates.
9. Regulatory reporting and cost
Because the event was a significant interruption lasting more than 24 hours, a summary 
report was due within five working days after restoration; it was filed on May 29, 2026.
Restoration cost is estimated at $38.4 million: $24.3 million of O&M recorded as a 
regulatory asset and $14.1 million of capital. System restoration costs can be securitized, 
but since September 1, 2025 the threshold is $50 million, so this event is expected to be 
recovered through rates rather than securitization.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
10. What worked and what did not
The May 6 drill had tested the hurricane annex and the staging sites two weeks earlier. 
Staging and material flow worked well once mutual-assistance crews arrived. The gaps 
were the timing of the mutual-assistance request, contact center capacity on May 20 and the 
loss of premise-level restoration estimates.
11. Actions
The review set eight actions. The four with the largest expected effect are listed below; 
owners and dates are tracked in the EP&R action log.
 Request mutual assistance earlier when forecast wind gusts exceed 60 mph.
 Store premise-level restoration estimates so accuracy can be measured.

Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
Materials and Storm-Stock Strategy: 
Distribution Transformers
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Supply Chain and Fleet | 2026-09-04 | v1.0
Memo to the Chief Operating Officer and the Chief Financial Officer from Supply Chain and 
Fleet, September 4, 2026; copy to the Vice President, Distribution Operations. Subject: 
distribution transformer stock and storm reserve. It explains the August stockouts, their 
effect on field work and the options for the rest of 2026.
Summary
In August 2026 three pad-mount transformer sizes fell below their reorder minimums, 
leaving only storm reserve stock. New-service and replacement work that needs those sizes 
is waiting. We ask for a decision on the options in section 6.
1. Stock position at August 31
3 of 146 stocked items were below their reorder minimum, all pad-mount transformers:
 Single-phase 50 kVA, 7.2 kV: 38 on hand against a minimum of 120, all held as storm 
reserve.
 Single-phase 100 kVA, 7.2 kV: 22 on hand against a minimum of 70, all held as storm 
reserve.
 Three-phase 500 kVA, 12.47 kV: 3 on hand against a minimum of 12, all held as storm 
reserve.
2. Effect on field work
At August 31, 87 work orders in Bayou and Crossroads were waiting for material, 71 of 
them transformer replacements, plus 9 pole replacements and 7 small new services. 
Another 34 were waiting for a planned outage.
3. Demand
Delivery points grew 1.5% from August 2025 to August 2026, with 13,152 new service 
points connected in 2025 and 8,337 from January to August 2026. The May wind event 
added 610 failed transformers.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
4. Supply
Distribution transformers come from two qualified suppliers, Supplier A (Larkspur Electric 
Products) and Supplier B (Tidewell Transformer Company). Quoted lead times for stocked 
transformers range from 30 to 104 weeks, with a median of 60 weeks.
Supplier B has indicated a fourth-quarter 2026 delivery of 400 single-phase 50 kVA pad-
mount units but has not confirmed the date in writing; we treat this delivery as 
unconfirmed.
This is an industry-wide constraint: a 2024 national study reported lead times of up to two 
years and price increases of four to nine times over three years, with an estimated 60 to 80 
million distribution transformers in service in the United States.
5. Storm reserve policy
Storm-critical items carry a storm reserve that is part of on-hand stock and can be released 
only by the storm materials lead or the VP Supply Chain and Fleet. Releasing reserve for 
routine work reduces the stock available for the rest of the hurricane season.
6. Options
 A. Raise reorder minimums for single-phase pad-mounts by about 40%.
 B. Release up to half of the storm reserve for new-service work until December 1.
 C. Qualify a third supplier.
 D. Repair or rewind selected returned units.
7. Cost
Raising minimums and the storm reserve for the three sizes would add about $6.2 million of 
inventory. Options B and D have no inventory cost but carry storm and quality risk.
8. Stock summary

146 items, and the average quoted lead time, follow. Quantities are in each item's stocking

files.filename: 2026-2028 Resiliency Plan: Progress Update for Communities.pdf
files.search:
2026-2028 Resiliency Plan: Progress Update for
 Communities
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Corporate Communications with Resiliency Program Office |
2026-09-21
Sedgewater is making its electric system in the Coastal Plain stronger against storms, heat and
flooding. This update explains the 2026-2028 Resiliency Plan, what we are doing in your district this
year and what we have finished so far.
What the plan is
The Public Utility Commission of Texas approved our 2026-2028 Resiliency Plan on October 23,
2025. It includes nine measures and about $612 million of investment over three years. Texas law
allows resiliency plans to use hardening, modernization, undergrounding, vegetation management
and other measures over at least three years.
Why it matters
On May 19, 2026 a line of severe thunderstorms with straight-line winds crossed our service area,
with the heaviest damage in Bayou and Prairie, and a second band of storms followed on the night
of May 20. Bayou's tree canopy and flood exposure, and Prairie's long rural lines, make those
districts the focus of much of the plan.
What we are doing in 2026
Replacing and bracing poles on Bayou and Prairie lines; adding automatic switching on lines that
serve hospitals, water plants and other critical facilities; building flood walls at two substations; and
trimming trees faster on high-risk lines, moving those lines to a three-year trimming cycle.
Progress so far
By the end of August 2026:
About 3,000 poles replaced or braced.
About 190 extra miles of tree trimming.
More than 110 automatic switching devices installed.
8 miles of line moved underground.
14 new weather stations in service.
Flood walls under construction at two substations.

The nine measures
Pole replacement and bracing; faster vegetation trimming; feeder automation; strategic
undergrounding; substation flood mitigation; underground cable replacement; transmission
structure hardening; weather stations and damage modeling; and substation physical security.
Our service area
Sedgewater serves the Coastal Plain service area in four districts: Harbor, Crossroads, Bayou and
Prairie. We deliver electricity for the retail electric providers our customers choose; outages and
hazards should be reported to Sedgewater.

Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
Gas Distribution Business Unit Profile
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Gas Operations | 2026-09-02 | v1.0
Profile of Sedgewater Gas Distribution for internal partners and the outside operations 
review: what the business does, its customers and system, how it is regulated and paid, and 
its current operating priorities. Prepared by the Vice President, Gas Operations, September 
2, 2026.
What we do
Sedgewater Gas Distribution buys natural gas, delivers it through its own mains and 
services, and bills its customers directly. Rates are set by municipalities with original 
jurisdiction inside their limits and by the Railroad Commission of Texas outside them, with 
the RRC hearing appeals of municipal decisions.
Customers
We served 262,300 customers at December 31, 2025: Crossroads 96,400, Bayou 117,800 
and Prairie 48,100. Harbor District has no Sedgewater gas service. The count was 262,100 
at July 31, 2026, reflecting normal summer move-outs.
Throughput is concentrated in winter: about two-thirds of annual volume moves in the first 
and fourth quarters.
System and people
At year-end 2025 the system had 4,980 miles of main (polyethylene 3,720, protected steel 
1,172, unprotected steel 84 and other plastic 4) and 251,000 services. Sedgewater Gas 
Distribution had 452 employees at June 30, 2026, with shared services provided by 
Sedgewater Services Company.
Revenue, rate base and rates
2025 operating revenue was $358 million, of which about $142 million was gas cost passed 
through to customers. Rate base was about $1.18 billion at December 31, 2025.
Gas cost changes pass through each month under the purchased gas adjustment, which lets 
rates follow the cost of gas. Capital between rate cases is recovered through annual interim 
rate adjustments, which we have filed since March 2023. The March 27, 2026 filing covered 
$86.4 million of 2025 net invested capital and requested an $11.2 million increase.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
A utility using interim adjustments must file a comprehensive rate case by the fifth 
anniversary of its first filing, so our next gas rate case is due by March 2028.
Leaks
In 2025 we found 2,040 leaks (164 grade 1, 551 grade 2 and 1,325 grade 3); 188 were 
caused by excavation damage. From January to August 2026 we found 1,360 (110 grade 1, 
368 grade 2 and 882 grade 3); 69 were caused by excavation damage.

monitored; the median grade 2 leak was resolved in 30 days. The table summarizes days to

files.title: Sedgewater Energy Delivery: Company Overview
files.search:
Sedgewater Energy Delivery: Company Overview
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Corporate Communications | 2026-09-01
Sedgewater Energy Holdings delivers electricity and natural gas to homes and businesses in the
Coastal Plain service area on the upper Texas Gulf Coast. This overview explains what we do,
where we work and who we are. Information is as of June 30, 2026 unless stated otherwise.
Who we are
Sedgewater Energy Holdings, Inc. is a Texas energy-delivery holding company headquartered in
Houston. It owns Sedgewater Electric Delivery, LLC, Sedgewater Gas Distribution, LLC and
Sedgewater Services Company.
The holding company was formed in 2002, when Texas electric restructuring separated its
predecessor's generation and retail businesses. Texas law required integrated electric utilities to
separate into a power generation company, a retail electric provider and a transmission and
distribution utility by 2002; Sedgewater kept the wires business and the gas distribution business.
What we do - electricity
Sedgewater Electric Delivery is a transmission and distribution service provider in the ERCOT
region. We build, operate and maintain poles, wires, substations and meters, restore outages and
process service orders. We do not generate electricity or sell it to end-use customers.
Customers buy electricity from one of 58 retail electric providers, who bill them and pay us
regulated delivery charges. ERCOT operates the regional grid and wholesale market, where
generators sell power and retail providers buy it; we coordinate transmission planning, outage
scheduling and emergency operations with ERCOT. As a transmission and distribution service
provider we are regulated by the PUCT and must provide non-discriminatory access to our system.
What we do - natural gas
Sedgewater Gas Distribution buys natural gas, delivers it through its own mains and services and
bills its customers directly. Its rates are set by municipalities with original jurisdiction and by the
Railroad Commission of Texas.
Where we work
Our fictional Coastal Plain service area is organized in four districts. Harbor is a port and industrial
corridor with dense older neighborhoods; Crossroads is our fastest-growing suburban district;
Bayou has older low-lying suburbs with heavy tree canopy; Prairie is rural and exurban with long
overhead lines. Gas service covers Crossroads, Bayou and Prairie.
Scale
About 683,000 electric delivery points and 262,200 gas customers at June 30, 2026.

About 1,240 circuit miles of 69 kV and 138 kV transmission lines.
2,612 employees: 1,540 at Sedgewater Electric Delivery, 452 at Sedgewater Gas Distribution and
620 at Sedgewater Services Company.
Where our people work
About 420 staff work at our Houston headquarters and about 780 at our Houston operations center,
which houses distribution control, outage management, storm command and our main contact
center. Field crews report to four district service centers and three gas service centers.
Leadership
Dana Whitfield, President and CEO; Marcus Oyelaran, COO; Priya Raman, CFO; Hannah Lowell,
General Counsel; Tomas Ybarra, VP Regulatory Affairs; Gareth Pruitt, VP Distribution Operations;
Renee Dufresne, VP Gas Operations; Kwame Asante, VP Asset Management and Engineering;
Denise Okafor, SVP Customer and Market Operations; Frank Lindqvist, VP Supply Chain and
Fleet.
Building resilience
Our 2026-2028 Resiliency Plan, approved by the PUCT in October 2025, includes nine measures
and about $612 million of capital over three years. After major storms we work with other utilities
through a regional mutual assistance group.

Board Executive Brief: 2027 Rate Case 
Timing and Capital Pacing
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Finance and Regulatory Affairs | 2026-09-19 |  
vBoard pre-read
Board executive brief for the October 8, 2026 meeting. Subject: timing of the next electric 
base rate case and capital pacing. Prepared by the Chief Financial Officer and the Vice 
President, Regulatory Affairs, September 19, 2026. Decision requested.
1. Decision requested
Management recommends filing the next electric base rate case in the second quarter of 
2027, using a 2026 test year. The alternative is to file in the fourth quarter of 2027 after a 
further DCRF update. The board is scheduled to decide at its October 8, 2026 meeting.
2. Where rates stand
The last electric base rate order (March 2022) set a 9.60% return on equity and a 42.5% 
equity ratio. Rate base was about $4.62 billion at December 31, 2025.
Since then capital has been recovered through DCRF and TCOS updates. A DCRF update is 
allowed no more than twice a year. We filed DCRF updates in April and September 2025; the 
first 2026 update ($41.8 million) took effect in July and the second, about $23 million, is 
planned for September 28.
3. Why file in 2027
Rate base has grown since the 2022 order; storm costs are below the securitization 
threshold and need a rate path; vegetation and contractor unit costs are higher than in 
current rates; and the second 2026 DCRF uses the last available DCRF update before rates 
are reset.
4. O&M pressure
2026 O&M is $8.5 million over budget through August ($364.5 million against $356.0 
million), and the full-year forecast is $556 million against a $541 million budget. The largest 
variances are Distribution Operations (+$4.4 million) and Vegetation Management (+$3.1 
million). The forecast is above budget mainly because of vegetation unit costs, contractor 
rates and outside regulatory costs. O&M actuals exclude storm costs recorded as regulatory 
assets.

can be securitized, but the threshold is $50 million, so both events need recovery through 
base rates.
6. Capital pacing
The 2026 capital budget is $1,120 million; $683.0 million was spent through August and the 
forecast is $1,108 million. The 2026-2030 outlook is about $6.10 billion.
The resiliency plan approved in October 2025 ($612 million of capital and $41 million of 
O&M over three years, against $890 million proposed) is on a separate recovery path.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • Board pre-read
2026 resiliency capital is forecast at $180 million against $196 million, mainly because 
undergrounding is behind; $109.0 million of capital and $3.37 million of O&M were 
recorded through August.
7. Gas
The gas utility must file a comprehensive rate case by March 2028 because its first interim 
rate adjustment was filed in March 2023. Filing electric in 2027 keeps the two cases about a 
year apart.
8. Risks of each option
 Second quarter 2027: larger regulatory workload in a hurricane season; the test year 
includes the May 2026 event.
 Fourth quarter 2027: one more DCRF update, but storm costs and higher O&M stay 
unrecovered longer, and the filing moves closer to the gas case.

Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
Information Package Cover Memo
Sedgewater Energy Holdings | Office of the Chief Operating Officer | 2026-
09-25 | v1.0
Cover memo from the Chief Operating Officer to the outside operations consultant, 
September 25, 2026. It explains what this information package contains, how the 
documents relate and what has been withheld.
Purpose
We assembled this package in September 2026 for your review of how planning, field work 
and regulatory reporting fit together at Sedgewater. The documents are working files as our 
teams use them, not documents prepared for the review, so some carry older dates or 
details that were later revised.
Who we are
Sedgewater Energy Holdings owns Sedgewater Electric Delivery, a transmission and 
distribution service provider in the ERCOT region that does not generate or sell electricity, 
and Sedgewater Gas Distribution, which buys, delivers and bills natural gas. Sedgewater 
Services Company provides shared services.
What is in the package
 Regulatory: the 2026 submissions calendar, the reliability metric standard and 2025 
reliability report, the EOP hurricane and flood annex excerpt, the 2026 vegetation plan 
and the draft pole plan.
 Procedures: work management, contractor requirements and gas leak management.
 Data workbooks: feeders and pole inspections, vegetation, work orders and crew hours, 
interruptions, capital, O&M, gas inventory and surveys, customer contacts and safety.
 Reviews and proposals: the May 2026 after-action review, Reliability Council, 
operations review, materials memo, resiliency checkpoint, capital overview, Harbor 
North proposal, meter pilot, gas profile, steel review, customer operations and safety 
summary.
 External and governance: REP service guide, community resiliency update, contractor 
forum, company overview, service area facts, lender update and the October board brief.
Notes on the data
The work-order extract covers Bayou and Crossroads only, the two districts that moved to 
the current WMS configuration first; crew hours cover all four districts.
Sedgewater Energy Holdings • 1.0
The regulatory calendar shows 61 submissions for 2026, 44 of them submitted by 
September 15, with one municipal report submitted two days late.
What we have withheld
Customer account and premise-level data, facility locations and maps, control-system 
details, security plans, personnel files and privileged legal material are not included. 
Distribution control and substation automation systems are outside the scope of the 
package.
Available on request
The next-generation meter pilot charter (approved February 2026), which defines the 
pilot's success measures, is available on request.
Contacts
Please route questions through my office; we will direct them to the document owners 
named in each file.
